Clinical Phenotypes and Prognostic Heterogeneity of Mild-to-Moderate Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Prospective Community-Based Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: The clinical phenotypes, prognosis, and heterogeneity of mild-to-moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have not been systematically evaluated. Do different clinical phenotypes of mild-to-moderate COPD have different prognoses? We analysed the baseline and 3-year follow-up data of participants with mild-to-moderate COPD from a prospective community-based cohort study. Mild-to-moderate COPD was defined as a forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) / forced vital capacity ratio of < 0.70 and FEV1 ≥ 50% of the predicted value. The clinical phenotypes included respiratory symptoms, exacerbation history, emphysema, air trapping, and airway remodelling. Respiratory health outcomes included exacerbations and lung function decline over the 3-year follow-up. Overall, 806 participants with mild-to-moderate COPD were included, of whom 712 (88%) completed the 3-year follow-up. Participants with mild-to-moderate COPD had more severe emphysema, air trapping, and airway remodelling; increased exacerbation risk; and faster annual FEV1 decline than those with preserved spirometry. The severity of airflow obstruction, respiratory symptoms, emphysema, and air trapping, as well as the eosinophilic phenotype, had low overlap in mild-to-moderate COPD. There was significant individual variation in the annual FEV1 decline rate and exacerbation incidence among participants with mild-to-moderate COPD. Emphysema and air trapping were associated with faster FEV1 decline and higher exacerbation risk. Respiratory symptoms and exacerbations in the previous year were associated with a higher acute exacerbation risk but not with faster lung function decline. Mild-to-moderate COPD exhibited distinct clinical phenotypes with significant prognostic heterogeneity. Accurate phenotype identification is essential for targeted intervention, clinical precision management, and prognostic improvement.

articles.title: European Society of Intensive Care Medicine consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit.
articles.abstract: A human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit (ICU) aims to integrate person-centred care, communication, emotional support, equity, and collaboration into ICU environments. The European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) developed a consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU following a systematic, multi-phase, evidence-informed methodology incorporating the views of ICU professionals, academics, and patient and family representatives. This international multidisciplinary panel of 46 members conducted rapid reviews addressing 20 Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes (PICO) questions across six domains: person-centred care; communication and transparency; emotional well-being; equity, diversity, and inclusion; ICU environment; technology and innovation. Based on the evidence synthesis, 53 draft statements were developed and evaluated through a two-round eDelphi study. The final set of statements was discussed and ratified at an expert consensus meeting with the initial panel of experts and with patients and family representatives. A total of 201 international stakeholders participated in round 1 and 149 in round 2. Members of the expert consensus meeting ultimately endorsed 43 consensus statements. Key recommendations supported flexible family visitation, structured interdisciplinary communication, empathy-based staff training, psychological support for patients and ICU professionals, culturally responsive care, environmental interventions to improve sleep and reduce delirium, and the integration of digital supported technologies. The consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU provides a comprehensive framework for clinicians with evidence-informed directions to deliver high-quality practice across diverse ICU settings. By prioritising person-centred care, communication, inclusivity, and well-being alongside responsible technological innovation, the experiences and outcomes of patients, families, and ICU professionals may improve.

articles.title: Restoring patients' voice in intensive care: augmentative and alternative communication for human-centred care.

Preliminary Exploration of the Hepatoprotective Effect of Nanocrystalline Curcumin Against Traumatic Hemorrhagic Shock-Induced Liver Injury in a Desert Dry-Heat Environment: A Network Pharmacology-Based Study.
articles.abstract: Traumatic hemorrhagic shock (THS) under desert dry-heat conditions can exacerbate secondary liver injury, highlighting the need for effective therapeutic interventions. This study investigated the protective effects of nanocrystalline curcumin (NC-Cur) against THS-induced liver injury in a desert dry-heat environment and explored its potential molecular mechanisms. Network pharmacology, Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment analyses, and protein-protein interaction network analysis were used to identify candidate targets. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations examined curcumin-protein interactions. Forty male Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly assigned to control, model, solvent, or NC-Cur treatment groups (n = 10 each). The model, solvent, and treatment groups underwent traumatic hemorrhagic shock under desert dry-heat conditions. Hepatic injury was assessed by histopathology, serum aminotransferases, inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress markers, and Western blotting. Network analysis identified 116 overlapping targets, with heat shock protein 90 alpha A1 (HSP90AA1), AKT serine/threonine kinase 1 (AKT1), and B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) prioritized as the core targets. Docking predicted favorable interactions with all three proteins, while molecular dynamics simulations supported stable binding between curcumin and HSP90AA1. Compared with untreated model rats, NC-Cur-treated rats showed attenuated hepatic histopathological injury, reduced alanine and aspartate aminotransferases, tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and malondialdehyde, and increased superoxide dismutase. Western blotting indicated reduced HSP90AA1 and increased phosphorylated AKT1 expression after NC-Cur treatment, with changes also observed in BCL-2 expression. These findings suggest that NC-Cur may alleviate liver injury associated with THS under desert dry-heat conditions in male rats, potentially involving HSP90AA1-AKT1-BCL-2-related signaling.

articles.title: Tongue capillary refill time and imaging parameters for acute coronary syndrome identification: A prospective ED study.
articles.journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
articles.abstract: Rapid identification of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in emergency department (ED) patients with chest pain remains challenging. Tongue capillary refill time (CRT) and tongue imaging may reflect systemic perfusion, but their value in ACS is unknown. To evaluate the diagnostic performance of standardized tongue-derived perfusion, macroscopic, and imaging parameters for identifying ACS. This prospective observational study enrolled 208 consecutive adult ED patients presenting with chest pain. Standardized tongue imaging and tongue CRT were assessed. A separate 20-patient pilot assessed interobserver reliability using ICC and kappa coefficients. Blinded ACS adjudication used clinical findings, serial high-sensitivity troponin measurements, electrocardiography, imaging studies, specialist consultations, and follow-up data. ROC analysis and multivariable logistic regression were performed. Among 208 patients, 61 (29.3%) had ACS: 16 STEMI, 41 NSTEMI, and four unstable angina cases. Tongue CRT was significantly prolonged in ACS patients (2.6 [2.2-2.9] vs. 1.3 [1.1-1.6] seconds; p<0.001). Tongue CRT demonstrated excellent discrimination for ACS (AUC 0.941, 95% CI 0.903-0.980), outperforming the HEART score (0.860), admission troponin (0.831), and TIMI score (0.788). A CRT threshold ≥2s yielded 86.9% sensitivity and 93.2% specificity. Tongue CRT and macroscopically dry tongue remained associated with ACS after adjustment (both p<0.001). Quantitative RGB and HSV parameters showed no significant between-group differences. Standardized tongue CRT showed excellent discrimination for ACS in this cohort, in which most ACS cases were myocardial infarction. Its diagnostic value in unstable angina and incremental clinical utility remain unestablished. External validation is required before routine clinical use.

articles.title: [Nursing competencies in ECMO care: a scoping review].
articles.abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is used in cases of refractory cardiac or pulmonary failure and places high demands on the treatment team, particularly on nursing staff, whose required competencies have scarcely been described in German-speaking countries. The primary aim was to map the international evidence on nursing competencies in the care of adult ECMO patients. Secondary aims included identifying specialised nursing roles and drawing implications for the German-speaking countries. The scoping review was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Joanna Briggs Institute and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses- Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The literature search was carried out in MEDLINE, CINAHL and Scopus, as well as in reference lists. German- and English-language primary studies published between 2009 and May 2026 were included. A total of n = 14 studies were included, comprising n = 7 qualitative (n = 6 [semi-structured] interview studies, n = 1 focus group interview) and n = 7 quantitative (n = 3 cross-sectional studies, n = 1 Delphi survey, n = 1 prospective cohort study, n = 1 prospective observational study, and n = 1 quasi-experimental study) studies. Based on the identified evidence, a multidimensional competency profile for ECMO nursing care can be described, including the necessary knowledge, practical skills, and professional attitudes. In addition, specialised nursing roles were identified. No studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified for German-speaking countries. A multidimensional competency profile emerges that is internationally anchored in specialised nursing roles; however, empirical data, role profiles and structured qualification pathways are lacking in German-speaking countries.

articles.title: A scoping review evaluating artificial intelligence applications across various injury prevention domains.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly utilized for injury prevention across diverse clinical and community settings including machine learning (ML). This scoping review aimed to synthesize the current literature on the applications and predictive performance of AI across multiple injury prevention domains. This scoping review searched five major databases, including PubMed, Embase, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, and the Cochrane Library, to identify studies evaluating AI applications for injury prevention published through May 2026. Eligible studies included original U.S.-based, English-language research across self-harm and suicide, abuse and violence, fall prevention, and sports injury prediction. Studies were excluded if they lacked measurable prevention outcomes or sufficient methodological detail, or focused on injury treatment rather than prevention, to ensure relevant and interpretable evidence for synthesis. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. ML models generally outperformed or matched traditional screening methods for self-harm and suicide prediction (AUC 0.81-0.82), while multimodal approaches achieved the highest predictive accuracy (AUC 0.90). In abuse and violence prevention, AI predicted intimate partner violence with an AUC of 0.88 and identified cases before formal disclosure. AI also improved fall risk assessment by accurately categorizing patient risk levels, predicting future falls, and mitigating fall injuries through wearable airbag technology. ML models predicted future sports-related injuries (AUC 0.76-0.84), while identifying modifiable risk factors including workload, strength deficits, prior injury burden, and concussion history. ML-based prediction showed promise for risk stratification in self-harm, suicide, intimate partner violence, and recurrent victimization. Additionally, AI predicted fall risk and identified athletes at risk for future sports-related injuries while detecting modifiable risk factors, including workload, prior injury burden, and strength deficits. Although these findings suggest that AI and ML may have potential applications in supporting earlier risk identification, informing targeted prevention strategies, and facilitating more personalized approaches to injury prevention, the limited available evidence warrants careful interpretation.

articles.title: Point-of-care ultrasound for confirming endotracheal tube placement in prehospital and critical care transport: a scoping review.
articles.abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has demonstrated high pooled diagnostic accuracy for endotracheal tube (ETT) placement confirmation in adult Emergency Departments and Intensive Care Units,, but its translation to pre-hospital and Critical Care Transport (CCT) environments is unclear. We mapped the published evidence on POCUS-based ETT placement confirmation in transport, organized around six axes: clinical indication, transport modality, operator training, impact on management, technical barriers, and patient-oriented outcomes. Scoping review per the Joanna Briggs Institute 2020 framework, reported per PRISMA-ScR. Nine sources searched January 1st, 2015-May 12th, 2026: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Europe PMC, Consensus.app, Google Scholar, ClinicalTrials.gov, and forward-citation tracking. Dual independent screening and charting were performed in Covidence with built-in conflict adjudication. From 2447 unique records, 51 met final inclusion. One primary study evaluated diagnostic performance in adult patients in an out-of-hospital setting. The remaining 50 records comprised contextual primary studies and secondary evidence, including cadaver and simulation studies, training evaluations, feasibility implementations, and reviews. Distribution by modality was skewed toward ground emergency medical services (EMS); rotor-wing helicopter EMS (HEMS) evidence was predominantly training-based; fixed-wing evidence was essentially absent. Operator profiles in transport-relevant studies were predominantly paramedic, flight medic, or flight nurse, mismatched against the physician-dominant pooled in-hospital meta-analytic estimates. No included study measured patient-oriented outcomes. Evidence supporting POCUS-based ETT confirmation in pre-hospital and critical care transport remains limited. Most studies addressed training, simulation, feasibility, or implementation rather than diagnostic performance in transported patients, and none demonstrated an effect on patient-oriented outcomes. Transport-specific prospective studies are needed before hospital-derived diagnostic-accuracy estimates can be generalized to transport practice.

articles.title: Naxos disease: current insights from early clinical observations to genetics and precision medicine.
articles.abstract: Naxos disease is the prototype of the Naxos disease cardiocutaneous spectrum, a group of inherited desmosomal disorders characterised by distinctive hair and skin abnormalities that precede the development of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM). Since its original clinical description in 1986 and the subsequent identification of the first ACM-causing gene (JUP), Naxos disease has provided fundamental insights into the pathogenesis, diagnosis and management of inherited desmosomal cardiomyopathies. This review provides current insights into the evolving clinical spectrum, encompassing the characteristic cutaneous signature, early electrical abnormalities, progressive structural myocardial remodelling, inflammatory ("hot-phase") episodes, ventricular arrhythmias and heart failure. We discuss the expanding genotype-phenotype relationships involving JUP, DSP and DSC2, highlighting how distinct genetic substrates influence ventricular involvement, disease severity and clinical outcomes while sharing common desmosomal mechanisms. Particular emphasis is placed on early clinical recognition, multimodality imaging, genetic diagnosis, risk stratification and lifelong multidisciplinary management. Finally, we discuss the emerging role of international collaborative registries, including NAXCARE, in generating prospective real-world evidence to refine genotype-informed surveillance, improve risk prediction and support precision medicine. Nearly four decades after its original description, Naxos disease has evolved from a rare inherited syndrome into the prototype of desmosomal cardiomyopathy, demonstrating how careful clinical observation can drive molecular discovery, precision medicine and improved patient care.

articles.title: Emergency Department-Administered Extended-Release Buprenorphine After Fentanyl Overdose Reversed by Emergency Medical Services With Naloxone.
articles.abstract: Emergency Medical Services (EMS) providers are on the frontline of the opioid epidemic and administered naloxone to reverse suspected overdose over 442,000 times in 2024. Interest in EMS-initiated sublingual (SL) buprenorphine (BUP) exists; however, initiation of month-long extended-release buprenorphine (XR-BUP) in the immediate postoverdose period has not yet been described. The high risk of death from repeat overdose in patients with opioid use disorder (OUD) could be reduced by administration of XR-BUP. The purpose of this case report is to highlight the utility of EMS-initiated SL-BUP followed by XR-BUP to potentially improve care linkage and adherence to medication-assisted OUD treatment. A bystander call to 911 dispatched a Basic Life Support (BLS) unit to an unresponsive 30-year-old man found with fentanyl-smoking paraphernalia. First responders administered 8 mg of intranasal naloxone. Paramedics arrived 8 min later and assessed the patient to be in opioid withdrawal with a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of 22. The patient reported using heroin or fentanyl and methamphetamine daily. After consent, paramedics administered 16 mg of SL-BUP. In the ED, an addiction medicine consult service administered a 300-mg monthly XR-BUP formulation. WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: We report that rapid transition from naloxone reversal of overdose and EMS initiated SL-BUP to month-long XR-BUP is possible during a single emergency medicine encounter using a stepwise clinical pathway. We hope our observations encourage further prospective study of the intervention described as this may link patients to medication assisted OUD treatment, which decreases mortality in patients with OUD.

articles.title: Massive Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding in an Adolescent Patient: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding in pediatric patients arises from diverse etiologies that vary across age groups. Although it is an uncommon cause of life-threatening hemorrhagic shock, prompt recognition and management are essential. Owing to the infrequency of hemorrhagic shock from GI bleeding in pediatrics, emergency physicians may lack familiarity with its diagnosis and management. Furthermore, multiple etiologies may coexist and may not be detected during the initial esophagogastroduodenoscopy, increasing the risk of premature diagnostic closure. A 17-year-old boy with a history of plaque psoriasis was transported by ambulance to the pediatric emergency department of an urban level one trauma center, presenting with copious hematemesis and hemodynamic instability. Initial resuscitation in the emergency department included blood transfusion, followed by admission to the pediatric intensive care unit. The first endoscopic evaluation by pediatric gastroenterology identified duodenal erosion; however, the patient experienced further large-volume bleeding out of proportion to these findings. A subsequent endoscopy revealed a Dieulafoy lesion, which was treated successfully. The patient was ultimately discharged home and has remained stable during long-term follow-up. WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: Although severe GI bleeding in pediatric patients is uncommon, emergency physicians must quickly identify hemorrhagic shock across all age groups and be familiar with the broad differential diagnoses that vary by age. Initial management must prioritize airway protection and hemodynamic stabilization as a bridge to definitive intervention. Clinicians should recognize the limitations of endoscopic gastroduodenoscopy and consider the potential for concurrent sources of bleeding that may necessitate additional intervention. © 2025 Elsevier Inc. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, artificial intelligence training, and similar technologies.

articles.title: Transanal Extrusion of Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt Tubing in a Pediatric Patient.
articles.abstract: Gastrointestinal perforation is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication of ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunts. Patients may have minimal or no abdominal symptoms despite bowel perforation and the risk of ascending central nervous system infection. A 12-year-old boy with hydrocephalus treated with a VP shunt presented to the Emergency Department after his parents discovered a segment of rubber tubing in his stool. He was afebrile, well appearing, neurologically at baseline, and without abdominal pain, vomiting, or symptoms of shunt malfunction. His abdominal examination was benign. A shunt series demonstrated an intact right-sided VP shunt and retained catheter fragments from a previously disconnected left-sided shunt, without an apparent abnormality of the functioning shunt. Despite the reassuring examination and radiographic findings, passage of shunt tubing per rectum raised concern for bowel perforation. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated, and urgent surgical exploration demonstrated that the functioning right-sided VP shunt had perforated the colon with formation of a fistulous tract. The shunt was externalized and the colonic defect repaired. Cerebrospinal fluid cultures subsequently grew gram-negative organisms, requiring complete shunt removal, external ventricular drainage, and prolonged antimicrobial therapy.Why Should an Emergency Physician Be Aware of This?: Transanal extrusion of VP shunt tubing should prompt immediate concern for bowel perforation even in an asymptomatic, well-appearing patient with reassuring initial imaging. Prompt recognition, broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy, and urgent neurosurgical and surgical consultation are essential because bowel perforation may permit ascending infection resulting in ventriculitis, meningitis, or sepsis.

articles.title: Real-Time Ultrasound Guided Paramedian Lumbar Puncture in the Pediatric Emergency Department.
articles.abstract: Pediatric lumbar puncture is often performed using the traditional landmark approach. The ultrasound-assisted approach has demonstrated benefit, but its efficacy is limited by the lack of real-time ultrasound needle guidance. The ultrasound-guided paramedian technique is a novel approach that allows for active ultrasound guidance of the needle into the spinal canal. We describe 2 cases of successful ultrasound-guided paramedian lumbar puncture in the pediatric emergency department.

articles.title: Association between the site of emergency care and patient-centered outcomes in patients with cancer: rationale and design of the French COVER cohort.
articles.journal: European journal of emergency medicine : official journal of the European Society for Emergency Medicine
articles.abstract: Patients living with cancer now account for a substantial and growing share of emergency department (ED) visits and carry a high burden of hospitalization and in-hospital death. Their acute presentations are frequently multifactorial - driven by disease progression, treatment toxicity, immunosuppression, or the decompensation of comorbid conditions. They may present with higher rates of complications because of novel therapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors and cellular therapies, whose emergency manifestations remain unfamiliar to many emergency physicians. Despite this growing importance, the unscheduled care of patients with cancer has received comparatively little dedicated research. How these patients are managed in the ED, how often the emergency physician can access the oncology medical record and goals of care, how the acute complications of new anticancer therapies present, and how a background of cancer should modify the diagnostic approach to everyday emergencies remain poorly characterized. To address these gaps, the Cohort of Onco-hematologic patients visiting the Emergency depaRtment was designed as a prospective, multicenter French cohort of consecutive adults with active cancer or in remission for less than 1 year, presenting to the ED for any reason. Enrollment took place across a national network of 76 EDs for two 1-week periods (summer 2025 and winter 2025-2026), with follow-up to 90 days, yielding a large sample of patients designed as a platform for multiple analyses. The primary aim of Cohort of Onco-hematologic patients visiting the Emergency depaRtment is to determine whether being managed in an ED located within the patient's own cancer referral center, rather than any other hospital, is associated with improvement in morbidity and mortality, captured by the number of days alive and out of hospital at 30 days. Beyond this primary aim, the cohort will support a broad research program on the place of the ED in the cancer care pathway, from patient profiling and pathway description to the emergency toxicities of anticancer drugs and the cancer-specific features of common presentations.

articles.title: Epidemiology, clinical profile, and outcomes of older patients with active cancer attending at Spanish emergency departments (EDEN-56 study).
articles.journal: European journal of emergency medicine : official journal of the European Society for Emergency Medicine
articles.abstract: Older adults with active cancer are increasing, clinically complex emergency department (ED) population, but large multicenter European data are limited. To describe the epidemiology, baseline characteristics, diagnoses, and outcomes of older patients with active cancer attending Spanish EDs, and assess whether associations between active cancer and short-term outcomes varied with age and sex. Secondary analysis of the Emergency Department and Elder Needs retrospective multicenter registry, including all patients aged greater than or equal to 65 years attending 52 Spanish EDs during 1-7 April 2019. Patients with and without active cancer were compared. Annualized incidence was extrapolated overall, by sex, and by age. Age-related patterns were modeled using restricted cubic splines. ED length of stay, hospitalization, length of hospitalization, and index-episode death. Age-by-cancer and age-by-sex interactions were assessed in unadjusted and multivariable models. Among 25 557 older ED patients, 4701 (18.4%) had active cancer. The estimated annualized incidence of ED presentations was 10 885 per 100 000 inhabitants aged greater than or equal to 65 years [95% confidence interval (CI): 10 576-11 200], higher in men (annualized rate ratio: 1.80, 95% CI: 1.70-1.91) and in the mid-to-late 80s. Patients with cancer had more severe comorbidity (58.9 vs. 12.9%), polypharmacy (26.6 vs. 21.3%), and walking handicaps (31.5 vs. 28.2%). Malignancy accounted for only 7.7% of ED diagnoses in the cancer group; infections, heart failure, and respiratory conditions were frequent. Active cancer was associated with longer median ED stay (4.0 vs. 3.3 h; adjusted difference: 0.3, 95% CI: 0.1-0.4), higher hospitalization [32.5 vs. 24.0%; adjusted odds ratio (OR): 1.34, 95% CI: 1.25-1.44], longer median hospitalization (7.5 vs. 6.9 days; adjusted difference: 0.5, 0.1-0.9), and higher index-episode mortality (5.5 vs. 2.5%; adjusted OR: 2.12, 95% CI: 1.81-2.50). Age significantly modified ED length of stay, hospitalization, and mortality, with significantly different age-related changes between patients with and without cancer. Among patients with cancer, age-related trajectories did not significantly differ by sex. Active cancer is common among older ED patients and associated with substantial resource use and worse short-term outcomes. These associations vary with age, supporting multidimensional assessment beyond chronological age or cancer status alone.

articles.title: Association between multiday emergency department boarding and higher in-hospital mortality: evidence from Brazil.
articles.journal: European journal of emergency medicine : official journal of the European Society for Emergency Medicine
articles.abstract: Emergency department (ED) boarding is a major driver of overcrowding and has been associated with adverse outcomes. However, little is known about the impact of multiday boarding delays, which are common in low- and middle-income countries. Retrospective cohort study using administrative hospital data aimed to examine the association between ED boarding time and in-hospital mortality. Adult patients admitted via the ED of Hospital de Clínicas de Porto Alegre, a large tertiary hospital in Brazil, between January 2022 and December 2023. ED boarding time, defined as the interval between the admission decision and the patient's physical departure from the ED. In-hospital mortality was evaluated using multivariable logistic regression with restricted cubic splines modeling boarding time as a continuous exposure, adjusting for age, sex, and triage acuity. Among 28 743 admissions, the median boarding time was 1.8 days (interquartile ranges 0.6-3.5). In-hospital mortality was 8.36%. Compared with patients in the first boarding quartile (median 0.19 days), those in the last quartile (median 4.92 days) had higher adjusted odds of death [odds ratio (OR) 1.15; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.05-1.25]. At the cohort median (1.8 days), each additional day of boarding was associated with a 6% increase in the odds of in-hospital death (OR 1.06; 95% CI 1.02-1.09). Prolonged ED boarding time was independently associated with increased in-hospital mortality, with no evidence of a safe threshold. Multiday delays represent a modifiable risk factor associated with excess mortality.

articles.title: Operational end-of-life trajectory categories among patients who died in the emergency department: associations with resuscitative and palliative care in a five-year retrospective cohort.
articles.abstract: Emergency departments (EDs) increasingly care for patients approaching the end of life, yet the relationships between patterns of decline and final ED care remain poorly characterised. The objective was to describe the distribution of retrospectively assigned trajectory-oriented categories among ED decedents and examine associations with care processes. This single-centre retrospective cohort study included adults who died in the ED between 2018 and 2022. Categories were acute event/low comorbidity (T1), terminal malignancy or pre-existing exclusive palliative/comfort-focused care (T2), advanced chronic disease with acute decompensation (T3), frailty/dementia or high comorbidity with severe functional dependency (T4), and residual unclassified cases (T5). Primary outcomes were CPR and documented initiation of exclusive palliative/comfort-focused care; documented end-of-life recognition or discussion was secondary. Of 628 patients, 1.3% were T1, 10.8% T2, 10.0% T3, 49.4% T4, and 28.5% T5. CPR ranged from 75% in T1 to 24% in T2 and T4 (p<0.001). Exclusive palliative/comfort-focused care was initiated in 35% of T2 and 11% of T3-T5 patients (p<0.001). End-of-life recognition or discussion ranged from 12% in T1 to 51% in T2 (p=0.034). Frailty and dementia represented the main trajectory of death in the ED, while nearly one-third of patients could not be classified within the predefined categories. A pragmatic trajectory-oriented framework may help interpret observed patterns of care. However, retrospective assignment and the large residual group make these findings hypothesis-generating; prospective validation is required before decision-support use.

Easy as 1-2-3! Point-of-Care Ultrasound Estimation of Parapneumonic Effusion Size Using Intercostal Spaces in the Pediatric Emergency Department.
articles.abstract: There is limited evidence on the ability of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) to quantify and characterize pediatric parapneumonic effusions. This study aimed to evaluate the agreement between lung POCUS and radiology ultrasound (RADUS) or chest x-ray (CXR) in determining effusion size and complexity in children presenting to the pediatric emergency department (ED). We studied patients aged younger than 18 years diagnosed with parapneumonic effusions at the Hospital for Sick Children between June 1, 2018, and December 1, 2024. Included patients had undergone a lung POCUS demonstrating a pleural effusion and a RADUS or CXR within 36 hours of their POCUS examination. Patients with suboptimal POCUS images were excluded. Using previously described criteria, we determined whether an effusion was "drainable" or "non-drainable" using the number of involved intercostal spaces as an estimate of effusion size. Our primary outcome was the rate of agreement between the POCUS estimation of effusion size to that of RADUS (or CXR if RADUS was unavailable) using Cohen Kappa statistic. We also compared the rate of agreement between POCUS and RADUS for effusion complexity and the time taken to complete both imaging modalities. Eighty-five cases were included in this study. POCUS agreed with RADUS substantially in its ability to quantify (κ=0.76) and characterize (κ=0.65) parapneumonic effusions. There was also substantial agreement between POCUS and CXR for estimating effusion size (κ = 0.71). The median time to complete POCUS was significantly shorter compared with RADUS (6 vs. 14 min; P=0.003). Using a simple method of counting involved intercostal spaces, our results support the use of lung POCUS for quantifying and characterizing parapneumonic effusions in the pediatric ED. Future research is needed to evaluate the generalizability of these findings and their impact on clinical outcomes.

Birthday Blues: Clinical Patterns of Emergency Department Visits Surrounding Birthdays.
articles.abstract: Smaller studies have suggested that patients are more likely to present to the emergency department around the time of their birthdays. However, no multi-year analysis has been performed within the U.S. to uncover a possible association between birthdays and presentation to the emergency department (ED). The objective of this study was to evaluate the overall frequency year after year of visits to the Emergency Department and the medical conditions most frequently encountered around the time of a birthday. We studied emergency department visits from May 2018 to May 2024 at a Level 1 Trauma Center in a metropolitan city in the U.S.. Our analysis assessed the interval before or after ED presentation with respect to a patient's birthday. We utilized timeframes of ± 7 days (7 d) of one's birthday, ± 14 days (14 d), and ± 30 days (30 d) for analysis. We then conducted a descriptive analysis comparing proportions, standardized ratios (SR), and obtaining predictive probabilities from a multivariate logistic regression model. Of the 310,047 unique ED visits from 2018 to 2024, 12,650 visits were within ±7d of a patient's birthday. There were a greater than expected number of presentations ±7 d for all genders and age groups (particularly those <18 years old), and for those identifying as Asians. When looking at the role of chief complaint, individuals with a chief complaint related to Psychiatric/Toxicology, Trauma, Dermatologic, and Musculoskeletal concerns had a higher incidence of ED presentation ±7 d. Across all populations, birthdays appear to be associated with an elevated risk of serious illness.

articles.title: Signs of Life and Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Multicenter Observational Study.
articles.abstract: The prognostic value of individual signs of life (SOLs) remains unclear in patients experiencing traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (t-OHCA). To describe clinical outcomes among patients with t-OHCA by the presence of each SOL at the scene. Data from the SOS-KANTO 2017 study, a multicenter prospective registry of OHCA cases treated between 2019 and 2021, were retrospectively analyzed. Adult patients diagnosed with t-OHCA were included, excluding those with a palpable pulse upon emergency medical service (EMS) arrival. Patients were categorized into eight subgroups based on the presence of three SOLs at the scene-the pupillary light reflex, spontaneous respiration, and cardiac electrical activity - and descriptive analyses were performed. The primary outcome was survival beyond the emergency department (ED). Of the 462 patients included in the analysis, two (0.4%) exhibited all three SOLs, and 18 (3.9%) exhibited two SOLs; in the latter group, two demonstrated cardiac activity and a pupillary reflex, and 16 had cardiac activity and spontaneous respiration. Among the 124 patients (26.8%) with only one SOL, 117 had cardiac activity, three showed a pupillary reflex, and four exhibited spontaneous respiration. No SOLs were observed in 318 patients (68.8%). Overall, 22 patients (4.8%) survived beyond the ED. The highest survival rate was observed in the subgroup with both cardiac activity and spontaneous respiration (4/16; 25%), followed by the subgroup with cardiac activity alone (10/117; 8.5%). Among the t-OHCA patients, survival beyond the ED was observed more frequently in those with cardiac electrical activity at the scene.

articles.title: Occlusion Myocardial Infarction Missed by ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) Criteria: An Angiographic Emergency Department Cohort.
articles.abstract: The ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)/non-STEMI (NSTEMI) paradigm uses ST-elevation as a surrogate for acute coronary occlusion, but ST-elevation criteria miss many occlusions. The occlusion myocardial infarction (OMI) vs. non-occlusion (NOMI) paradigm classifies patients by the presence of an acute occlusion. To compare the 2 paradigms in an angiography-selected emergency department (ED) cohort of acute myocardial infarction. Retrospective single-center cohort of consecutive adults given an ED diagnosis of STEMI or NSTEMI who underwent coronary angiography between December 2021 and October 2023. OMI was defined as an acute culprit lesion with thrombolysis in myocardial infarction (TIMI) 0 to 2 flow, or culprit stenosis above 70% with a peak emergency department high-sensitivity troponin I above 10,000 ng/L. Of 1052 patients, 458 (43.5%) were STEMI and 594 (56.5%) NSTEMI; 837 (79.6%) met the study OMI definition. The OMI definition was met by 430 of 594 NSTEMI patients (72.4%), and 430 of 837 OMI patients (51.4%) were STEMI-negative; 51 of 458 STEMI patients (11.1%) had no occlusion. Median peak ED troponin was 155 ng/L in STEMI(+)OMI and 639 ng/L in STEMI(-)OMI (p < 0.001); median ejection fraction was 50% in both (p = 0.004). Angiography within 2 h was performed in 85.7% of STEMI(+)OMI and 15.6% of STEMI(-)OMI patients (p < 0.001). In this angiography-selected cohort, more than half of the patients who met the study OMI definition were STEMI-negative, and these patients reached angiography far later than STEMI-positive patients with occlusion. Whether such patients can be recognized before angiography requires prospective validation of prespecified electrocardiogram (ECG) criteria.

articles.title: Temporal Patterns of Sexual Assault Presentations in U.S. Emergency Departments: Implications for Staffing and Forensic Readiness.
articles.abstract: Sexual assault (SA) remains a major public health issue, yet only a fraction of survivors seeks acute medical care in emergency departments (EDs). Although previous studies describe demographic disparities among SA survivors, national patterns of ED arrival timing and their operational implications for emergency care systems remain poorly characterized. To characterize the demographic and temporal patterns of ED presentations for SA in the United States. We conducted a repeated cross-sectional study using the Epic Cosmos database, including U.S. ED encounters related to SA from January 1, 2016 through December 31, 2024. Demographic characteristics and arrival patterns were compared with those of all other ED visits using odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Temporal distributions by day of week and 6-h arrival intervals were analyzed using chi-square testing and standardized Pearson residuals. Among 391,352,267 ED visits, 245,475 (0.06%) involved SA evaluation. Patients presenting with SA were disproportionately adolescents and young adults, female, Medicaid-insured, and from minoritized racial groups. Overnight arrivals (00:00-05:59) had significantly higher odds of SA presentation (OR, 1.45; 95% CI, 1.43-1.47), with peak presentations occurring on Sundays and Saturdays overnight. Morning presentations were consistently below expected levels. In 2016, 16% of patients presenting with SA arrived by ambulance; by 2024, this number had increased to 18%. SA presentations revealed distinct demographic and temporal patterns with important operational implications for EDs. Young and socially vulnerable populations are disproportionately affected. The concentration of presentations during overnight weekend hours highlights the need for expanded access to trauma-informed forensic services, including SA Nurse Examiner coverage and prehospital education, especially during high-demand periods.

articles.title: Muscle or Subcutaneous Fat? A Prospective Ultrasonographic Study of Dorsogluteal Injection Accuracy in the Emergency Department.
articles.abstract: Dorsogluteal intramuscular (i.m.) injection is commonly used in emergency departments, but successful delivery into muscle tissue may vary depending on patient anatomy. This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy of dorsogluteal i.m. injections performed in the emergency department using immediate postinjection ultrasonography and to identify factors associated with successful i.m. deposition. This prospective observational study was conducted in the dedicated injection area of a tertiary care emergency department between June 1 and June 15, 2018. Adult patients receiving dorsogluteal i.m. injections were consecutively enrolled. After exclusions, 134 patients were included in the study. The primary outcome was ultrasonographic determination of whether the injectate was deposited in the i.m. or subcutaneous (s.c.) plane. To address interobserver reliability, 20 additional consecutive patients receiving injections underwent independent ultrasonographic assessment by both radiologists, each blinded to the other radiologist's classification. Agreement was summarized using overall percentage agreement and Cohen's κ with a 95% confidence interval (CI), where estimable. Of the 134 patients, 72 (53.7%) were men. Ultrasonography reported that 82 injections (61.2%) reached the i.m. plane, whereas 52 (38.8%) remained in the s.c. tissue. Successful i.m. deposition was significantly more frequent in men than in women (88.9% vs. 29.0%, p < 0.001). s.c. tissue thickness and combined skin-plus-s.c. tissue thickness reported stronger discrimination for s.c. deposition than body mass index (BMI). In the additional 20-patient dual-ultrasound reliability cohort, the radiologists agreed on the clinically dichotomized injection outcome (correct i.m. vs. incorrect s.c./s.c.-i.m. deposition) in 19 of 20 examinations (95.0%), with a Cohen's κ of 0.875 (95% CI, 0.638-1.000), indicating almost perfect agreement. A considerable proportion of dorsogluteal injections performed in the emergency department do not reach the target muscle tissue. Direct regional s.c. tissue thickness seems to be a more clinically informative determinant of injection success than BMI alone.

articles.title: The Benefit of Early Advanced Airway Management Depends on Prehospital Epinephrine Timing in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: The combined effect of epinephrine and advanced airway management (AAM) timing on out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) outcomes remains poorly characterized. To investigate the interaction between epinephrine and AAM timing and their joint association with neurological and survival outcomes in OHCA. This retrospective study used Korea OHCA Registry data (August 2019-December 2023). We included adults receiving prehospital epinephrine and AAM. Epinephrine timing was early (=10 min) or late (>10 min) from emergency medical services arrival; AAM timing was early (=6 min) or late (>6 min). This yielded four groups: early epinephrine/early AAM (EE-EA), early epinephrine/late AAM (EE-LA), late epinephrine/early AAM (LE-EA), and late epinephrine/late AAM (LE-LA). Multivariable logistic regression and interaction analyses were performed for good neurological recovery (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2), survival to discharge, and prehospital return of spontaneous circulation. Of 20,662 eligible patients, 37.1% were in the EE-EA group. Compared with LE-LA, the EE-EA group had significantly higher odds of good neurological recovery (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.93-3.08) and survival to discharge (aOR 2.18, 95% CI 1.87-2.55). The LE-EA group showed no significant benefit over LE-LA (aOR 0.99, 95% CI 0.71-1.40). A significant interaction between early epinephrine and early AAM was observed for neurological recovery (aOR 1.45, 95% CI 1.08-1.95; p=0.045). Early epinephrine combined with early AAM was associated with optimal neurological recovery. However, this multiplicative interaction was attenuated in sensitivity analyses addressing resuscitation time bias, suggesting a hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory association.

articles.title: Corrigendum to "Is Our Understanding of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State Accurate?" [The Journal of Emergency Medicine, Volume 79, December 2025, Pages 531-538].
"Wax on, Wax off".
articles.abstract: Mentors play a profound role in professional development, providing guidance, confidence, stability, and a sense of belonging. Yet the sudden loss of a mentor can leave a protégé untethered, especially when the relationship extends beyond professional guidance into the fabric of one's personal and professional identity. Drawing on the author's experience of unexpectedly losing a long-standing mentor, this reflection explores the grief and disorientation that can accompany the end of an important mentoring relationship. While painful, losing a mentor can reveal mentorship's lasting influence and prompt a transition from being mentored to becoming a mentor.

articles.title: Discharge to Street.
On Whether the Sickest Patient in the Emergency Department Is in the Waiting Room.
articles.abstract: One common maxim in clinical medicine is that the sickest patient in the emergency department may be in the waiting room (termed the waiting-room maxim). The purpose of this commentary is to discuss 5 pitfalls related to the waiting-room maxim that can sometimes transform a fundamentally smart idea into a popular misconception. Brevity makes a maxim powerful, yet also creates limitations by leaving out elaboration, logic, and evidence.

articles.title: Utility of Routine Testing in Asymptomatic Markedly Elevated Blood Pressure in the Emergency Department: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Routine diagnostic testing for asymptomatic adults with markedly elevated blood pressure (BP) in the emergency department (ED) imposes a substantial operational burden despite uncertain clinical benefit. This study aimed to evaluate the prevalence and clinical significance of routine test abnormalities, identify predictors of actionable findings, and assess short-term clinical outcomes in this population. We conducted a prospective observational cohort study from May 2025 to February 2026. Asymptomatic adults (>18 years) with significantly elevated BP (systolic >180 mmHg or diastolic >110 mmHg) were enrolled. Acute target-organ damage (TOD) was ruled out using a structured symptom checklist. Primary outcomes were clinically meaningful test abnormalities and 7-day adverse clinical events. Among 210 enrolled patients (median presenting BP 199/118 mmHg), repeat measurement after >30 min showed a significant spontaneous median systolic reduction of 24 mmHg without acute intervention. While 13.3% of patients had clinically meaningful abnormalities, only 3.3% necessitated hospital admission and 3.3% required immediate treatment modification. Most abnormalities (10.9%) triggered process-driven outcomes, such as specialist consultations, without altering ED disposition. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) was the sole independent predictor of actionable findings (aOR = 8.28, (95% CI: 2.09-32.82; p = 0.003). The 7-day adverse event rate was low (1.9%), with no deaths or events occurring in patients without meaningful ED-based abnormalities. Routine screening for asymptomatic severe hypertension is low-yield and often identifies subacute conditions rather than emergencies. Validating 2025 American Heart Association (AHA)/American College of Cardiology (ACC) guidelines, a risk-stratified approach prioritizing CKD screening and rapid outpatient follow-up ensures safety while optimizing emergency resources.

articles.title: Renal Point-of-Care Ultrasound as a Screening Tool for Ureterolithiasis in Emergency Department Patients With Pyelonephritis.
articles.abstract: Pyelonephritis with concurrent ureterolithiasis is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, yet data on using point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) to evaluate these patients are limited. To evaluate the utility of hydronephrosis on POCUS to identify ureterolithiasis in patients with pyelonephritis. This retrospective study included patients 18 years or older presenting to a tertiary care emergency department (ED) between January 2015 and April 2025, diagnosed with pyelonephritis, who had a renal POCUS. Patients were excluded if they lacked flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness, had no urinalysis, or had incomplete imaging data. The primary outcome was diagnostic performance metrics of hydronephrosis on POCUS for identifying ureterolithiasis in patients with pyelonephritis. Secondary analyses included urinalysis results, ED length of stay (LOS), time to imaging completion, and return ED visits within 2 weeks. Of 439 patients identified, 363 were included; 173 received POCUS alone, and 190 received both POCUS and computed tomography (CT). Ureterolithiasis was identified in 25 patients (6.9%). In the combined cohort, hydronephrosis on POCUS demonstrated 84.0% sensitivity and 85.2% specificity for ureterolithiasis, with a negative predictive value of 98.6%. Median LOS for discharged patients receiving POCUS alone was 135 min shorter than those receiving both POCUS and CT (241.5 vs. 376.5, p< 0.0001). In this retrospective cohort of ED patients with pyelonephritis who underwent renal POCUS, absence of hydronephrosis on renal POCUS was associated with a lack of concurrent ureterolithiasis. Renal POCUS alone had a shorter ED LOS; however, further studies are needed to determine the efficacy and safety of a POCUS-guided approach.

articles.title: Validation of Diagnostic Scoring Systems in Patients With Clinical Suspicion of Necrotizing Soft Tissue Infection: A Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Several scoring systems have been developed and are used to aid in the differentiation of necrotizing soft tissue infection (NSTI) from non-necrotizing soft tissue infections; however, their diagnostic performance in patients with clinical suspicion of NSTI requiring surgical evaluation remains uncertain. To validate the diagnostic performance of commonly used scoring systems in patients presenting with clinical suspicion of NSTI and requiring surgical evaluation. We conducted a retrospective cohort study at a tertiary referral center from September 2018 to December 2022. Adult patients presenting to the emergency department with clinical suspicion of NSTI and subsequent surgical consultation were included. The diagnostic performance of Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC), modified LRINEC (MLRINEC), Japanese LRINEC (J-LRINEC), and SIARI (Site other than lower limb, Immunosuppression, Age, Renal impairment, and Inflammatory markers) scores was evaluated. A total of 359 patients were included, including 214 with NSTI and 145 with non-necrotizing soft tissue infections. Patients with NSTI had significantly higher LRINEC, MLRINEC, and J-LRINEC scores than those without NSTI (all p < 0.001). However, substantial overlap in score distributions was observed between groups. The areas under the curve (AUCs) were 0.663 for LRINEC, 0.693 for MLRINEC, 0.720 for J-LRINEC, and 0.486 for SIARI. Although higher score thresholds demonstrated relatively high specificity, sensitivity remained suboptimal across all evaluated scoring systems. Although several scoring systems demonstrated statistically significant differences between groups, substantial overlap remained between NSTI and severe non-necrotizing SSTIs, indicating that these scores should not be used as standalone diagnostic tools.

articles.title: Predictive Value of the Hemorrhage After Thrombolysis Score for Tissue Plasminogen Activator-Related Intracranial Hemorrhage: Emergency Department Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) improves outcomes in acute ischemic stroke but carries a risk of intracranial hemorrhage, particularly parenchymal hematoma (PH), which is associated with poor prognosis. Early risk stratification remains clinically important. To evaluate the diagnostic performance of the Hemorrhage After Thrombolysis (HAT) score in predicting PH following intravenous tPA in the emergency department. This secondary analysis included a single-center retrospective cohort conducted between October 2023 and February 2025. Adult patients with acute ischemic stroke treated with intravenous tPA within 4.5 h were included. Baseline clinical, laboratory, and imaging data were collected. The primary outcome was PH on 24-h cranial computed tomography. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, with the optimal cutoff determined by the Youden index. A total of 120 patients were included (mean age 70.2 ± 13 years; 57.5% male). PH developed in 11 patients (9.17%). HAT scores were significantly higher in the PH group (p < 0.001). The HAT score showed good discriminative performance for PH (area under the curve [AUC]: 0.871), with an optimal cutoff of 1 (sensitivity 82.6%, specificity 90.9%). For overall hemorrhagic transformation, performance was also good (AUC: 0.786). PH was associated with increased mortality and morbidity. The HAT score demonstrates good diagnostic performance for predicting PH after thrombolysis. It may serve as a practical tool for risk stratification and post-treatment monitoring in the emergency department.

articles.title: Identifying Opportunities to Strengthen Alignment Between Educational Mission and Faculty Effort in Pediatric Emergency Medicine.
articles.abstract: Pediatric emergency medicine (PEM) clinician educators (CEs) face challenges in balancing clinical, educational, and scholarship expectations. We describe an early-stage, Division-level program evaluation to support CE faculty in teaching and advancement. From August 2025 to April 2026, an Education Faculty Task Force (EFTF) was convened within an academic emergency department at a freestanding quaternary care children's hospital. The EFTF conducted a program evaluation incorporating (1) Division-level governance and College of Medicine promotion documents; (2) trainee evaluations; (3) a Division-wide survey; (4) a PEM fellow listening session; (5) a focused search of the external literature on education value unit models; and (6) an environmental scan of Division-level education structures within the Department of Pediatrics. We synthesized these data using concepts from complex adaptive systems and professional identity formation theories to identify areas of evidence convergence and inform implementation recommendations. The Division appointed 22 new CE faculty since 2020 and trains ~300 learners annually. Division educational governance was organized around programmatic roles with reporting lines directly to the Division Chief. A focused literature search on educational value units identified both benefits and barriers to sustained educator engagement. Within the Department of Pediatrics, heterogeneity existed in Division-level educational tracking and faculty engagement, reflecting local needs with no easily replicable model. Division-level programs involving simulation, interprofessional education, and procedural teaching demonstrated programmatic strengths but fragmentation. Strengthening educational infrastructure was deemed essential to support learners and sustainable CE scholarship. From these findings, the EFTF identified 5 priority implementation recommendations. As academic medical centers grow in scale and complexity, thoughtful institutional support of PEM CEs is imperative. We utilized a systems-oriented approach to identify opportunities for improving educational infrastructure while accounting for structural barriers, local communities of practices, and professional identity, with the goal of supporting an engaged and sustainable academic workforce.

articles.title: Analgesic use and pain burden in adults with major burns: A retrospective analysis.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: Pain control in severe burns remains challenging due to physiological factors affecting drug metabolism and efficacy. This study characterizes the most frequent combinations of pain medication, dosages of opioids and non-opioids over time, and their correlation with pain management in adults. A single-center retrospective analysis of patients ≥ 18 years of age admitted to University of North Carolina Jaycee Burn Center with ≥ 20% total body surface area (TBSA) burn injury between 2020 and 2024 was performed. Records were abstracted for demographics, prescription pain medication management, and numerical rating scale (NRS) pain scores. Generalized linear and mixed models assessed average daily pain scores and morphine milligram equivalents (MME), adjusted for age, TBSA burn, and inhalation injury. 140 patients were included (age: 32 ± 7 years; 72% male; TBSA burn 37 ± 19% [range: 20-98%]; length of stay: 42 ± 54 days; 19% inhalation injury). 88% survived and most injuries were flame-related (76%). Opioid-only regimens accounted for 7% of prescribing medications, non-opioid-only 15%, and multimodal regimens 78%. Acetaminophen and hydromorphone were most frequently administered (17%), followed by acetaminophen, hydromorphone, and oxycodone (14%) and acetaminophen, fentanyl, and oxycodone (13%). Patients receiving multimodal or opioid-only regimens demonstrated lower and more stable pain trajectories than those receiving non-opioids alone. Hydromorphone use increased with burn severity and was highest in patients with > 80% TBSA. Although opioid requirements declined over time, patients with burns > 40% TBSA had significantly higher MME at day 25 compared with moderate burns (451 ± 980 vs 237 ± 388; p = 0.023). Multimodal analgesia predominated and was associated with improved pain stability. Persistent opioid requirements in larger burns highlight the impact of burn-related metabolic alterations and support development of individualized analgesic strategies to optimize dosing and reduce prolonged opioid exposure.

articles.title: Exploring Canadian electrical injury survivors' and caregivers' experiences with recovery in Ontario: A qualitative study.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: This qualitative study aimed to: (1) describe electrical injury (EI) survivors' and caregivers' experiences with navigating daily life after an EI and (2) explore EI survivors' and caregivers' experiences with social support during recovery. Semi-structured interviews were conducted. Interviews were audio recorded, transcribed and analyzed thematically. Qualitative descriptive design. Sixteen participants (12 survivors, 4 caregivers) who were treated at Sunnybrook Hospital or St. John's Rehab between 2000-2020 were recruited to participate in the study. Recovery trajectories were marked by uncertainty, with survivors and caregivers describing complex physical, neurological, neuropsychological, psychological, and social challenges. Across interviews, participants emphasized the burden of 'invisible' symptoms, including cognitive, emotional, and function-limiting difficulties that were often difficult for others to recognize or predict. Survivors emphasized the need for diverse support networks, while caregivers expressed emotional and informational needs. Peer and naturally occurring social supports proved critical, with engagement influenced by individual, social, and environmental factors. This study underscores the unique and multifaceted challenges faced by EI survivors and their caregivers, highlighting the critical importance of addressing both physical and psychosocial recovery. In clinical practice, these findings emphasize the need for a comprehensive, multidisciplinary approach that integrates medical management with psychological support and social services.

articles.title: Effect of early burn wound cooling with tap water and hydrogel on clinical outcomes in scald injuries.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: This study aimed to assess the effects of first aid methods, including early burn wound cooling with running tap water and/or Burnshield® hydrogel, versus no treatment or inappropriate first aid on clinical outcomes in patients with scald burns. In this single-center retrospective analysis, we compared cooling first aid (defined as cooling with running tap water and/or hydrogel within 8 h after injury) with inappropriate or no first aid in 2566 patients with scald burns. Outcomes included time to complete epithelialization, surgical debridement, split-thickness skin grafting, systemic antibiotic use, hospitalization, age-stratified effects (pediatric/adult/geriatric), the effect of combining water with hydrogel, and timing of hospital admission. Overall, 73.4% of patients received cooling first aid. Median healing time was significantly shorter in the cooling first aid group 11 (8-14) days compared with the inappropriate first aid group 16 (12-23) days and the no first aid group 16 (12.25-23) days (p < 0.001). Cooling first aid was also associated with lower rates of debridement (17.05%), grafting (5.20%), systemic antibiotic use (11.84%), and hospitalization (17.26%) compared with inappropriate or no first aid (all p < 0.001). Median healing time differed by age group, with values of 12 (8-15) days in pediatric patients, 12 (8-15) days in adults, and 17 (12-23) days in geriatric patients (p < 0.001). The combination of tap water plus hydrogel yielded the shortest median healing time 10 (7-13) days and the lowest intervention rates. Admission within 24 h was associated with significantly better outcomes than later admission. Early cooling first aid substantially improves clinical outcomes in patients with scald burns. These findings support the effectiveness of hydrogel-based cooling as an adjunct to water irrigation and highlight the need for widespread public education on evidence-based first aid practices.

articles.title: Experimental study on the treatment of mouse burn injury combined with smoke inhalation injury using thrombopoietin.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: Burn injuries complicated by smoke inhalation significantly increase clinical severity and can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Inhalation injury is predominantly caused by exposure to toxic combustion gases, with thermal damage from steam being relatively uncommon. Thrombocytopenia is frequently observed in severe burns and is associated with poor outcomes, whereas platelet transfusion can carry clinically important risks. Recombinant human thrombopoietin (rhTPO), a hematopoietic growth factor used clinically for thrombocytopenia, may represent an alternative strategy for improving platelet-related recovery after burn-associated inhalation injury. Female C57BL/6 mice were subjected to a 30% total body surface area (TBSA) full-thickness burn combined with smoke inhalation injury. Mice were randomized into three groups: injury-only control, rhTPO subcutaneous injection group (SIG), and rhTPO nebulized inhalation group (NIG). Treatments commenced 0.5 h post-injury and continued for 3 days. Outcomes included 120-hour survival, arterial blood gas parameters, platelet count, thromboelastography, lung histopathology scores, plethysmography-based pulmonary function, and lung cytokine profiles. Both rhTPO administration routes improved 120-hour survival, increased platelet counts, and improved selected thromboelastography parameters. H&E-based histological assessment showed lower lung injury scores at later time points, and plethysmography-based respiratory parameters improved by 120 h. IL-1β and TNF-α levels were lower in rhTPO-treated groups, whereas IL-6 did not show a consistent decrease and should be interpreted cautiously. rhTPO administration, via either systemic or inhaled route, improved survival and several physiological and histological outcomes in this murine model of burn with smoke inhalation injury. Because this study did not include a healthy/sham control group or direct assays of platelet activation, pulmonary microthrombi, or rhTPO pharmacokinetics, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of therapeutic association rather than proof of a defined anti-inflammatory mechanism beyond the measured platelet-related changes.

articles.title: Determinants of fractional CO2 laser therapy utilization: Demographic, clinical, and psychosocial predictors.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: Fractional CO2 laser therapy (FCO2LT) is an effective treatment for hypertrophic scars (HTS); however, access and utilization remain low. A retrospective cohort of 3282 patients initially admitted to or treated at an ABA-verified burn unit within a level 1 trauma center (2017-2025), including those referred to affiliated institutions, was analyzed. Demographic, clinical, and insurance data were compared between patients who received FCO2LT and non-laser controls. Multivariable regression analyses identified the predictors of treatment, time to initiation, and number of sessions. A total of 3282 burn patients were included, of whom 290 (8.8%) received FCO2LT (mean age 31.6 years). Patients undergoing FCO2LT were younger (P < 0.01), more frequently female (P < 0.01), and more often Hispanic/Latino or Asian (P < 0.01), with the majority insured through Medicaid (P < 0.01). In the multivariable analysis, younger age, female sex, and insurance were associated with higher odds of FCO2LT, while non-White racial/ethnic groups collectively had lower adjusted odds compared with White/Caucasian patients (OR 0.939, P < 0.001). Among FCO2LT recipients, greater TBSA (P < 0.001), psychiatric history (P = 0.006), and insurance (P = 0.006) predicted more sessions, while younger age (P < 0.001) was associated with a longer time to initiation and psychiatric history (P = 0.003) with earlier initiation. Psychiatric history was independently associated with earlier initiation and greater number of treatments, underscoring the psychosocial drivers of scar care. Consistent coverage policies, particularly through Medicaid, facilitate access, whereas variability among private insurers remains a barrier. Both clinical and insurance factors strongly influenced FCO2LT utilization, emphasizing that access is shaped by systems as much as patient needs.

articles.title: "I had to have a couple of days off work to get there": Stakeholder perspectives in developing an occupational therapy burns telehealth service.
articles.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
articles.abstract: Telehealth models have the potential to help overcome challenges associated with the provision of in-person adult occupational therapy (OT) burn care. This study aimed to examine clinician and consumer perceptions of in-person adult burn care within a large adult burns service and explore the key features required to develop and implement an adult OT burns telehealth (OT TeleBurns) model of care. Interviews were conducted with adults after burn injury (n=23), and occupational therapists providing burn care to patients at their local facilities (n=18). Data were analysed first qualitatively to identify challenges with current in-person services, then coded using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) 2.0, to identify barriers and facilitators for implementing an adult OT TeleBurns service. Patient travel, local clinical expertise, communication across facilities, and patient attendance were key challenges of in-person services. CFIR constructs identified as strong facilitators for an OT TeleBurns service were the tension to change from in-person services, the relative advantage of telehealth services, and the proposed service's adaptability to the local context and ability to meet participants' needs. Perceived implementation facilitators were ensuring choice of appointment type, building local clinician capability, optimising communication methods, and establishing service governance and clear operational processes. Findings highlight strong support for developing an OT TeleBurns service given significant challenges with in-person care. Existing facilitators indicate high feasibility for implementation with clear clinical pathways and service procedures critical to ensuring an effective and sustainable model. Findings will be used to guide telehealth service development.
