articles.title: Inflammation and thrombosis: from pathophysiology to future treatments.
articles.abstract: Inflammation and coagulation are tightly interconnected host-defense systems that, when dysregulated, promote pathological thrombosis. This narrative review examines mechanisms, clinical settings, and therapeutic implications of thromboinflammation (TI) across venous, arterial, and microvascular thrombosis, with particular attention to the differences in clinical translation among vascular territories. Endothelial activation, tissue factor expression, platelet-leukocyte interactions, neutrophil extracellular traps, complement activation, inflammasome signalling, and impaired fibrinolysis converge to generate a procoagulant phenotype. These mechanisms modify Virchow's triad and contribute to venous, arterial, and microvascular thrombosis, although their relative importance varies across vascular territories. Clinically, TI is relevant in inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatologic and other immune-mediated disorders, sepsis, coronavirus disease 2019, clonal haematopoiesis, complement-mediated diseases, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. TI offers a unifying framework for mechanistic risk assessment and therapeutic development. In atherothrombosis, randomised trials have demonstrated that selective modulation of inflammatory pathways, particularly the NLRP3-interleukin-1β-interleukin-6 axis and colchicine-sensitive pathways, can reduce recurrent cardiovascular events. By contrast, the role of inflammation-targeted therapies for primary or secondary prevention of VTE remains uncertain. Future studies should identify disease-specific biomarkers and test targeted anti-inflammatory or immunothrombotic strategies, alone or alongside anticoagulation, to prevent thrombosis without compromising haemostasis effectively.

articles.title: Performance of pulmonary embolism diagnostic strategies in patients undergoing computed tomography pulmonary angiography.
articles.abstract: Clinical probability scores and D-dimer-based diagnostic strategies are intended for early evaluation of suspected pulmonary embolism (PE), but their performance after clinician-driven referral for computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) remains uncertain. We prospectively evaluated PE diagnostic strategies among consecutive emergency department patients aged ≥13 years who underwent CTPA for suspected PE. Following the decision to order CTPA, the modified Wells and simplified revised Geneva scores were calculated, and the YEARS and PEGeD strategies were applied. Clinically significant PE, defined as segmental or more proximal embolism, was the primary outcome; any PE, including isolated subsegmental embolism, was the secondary outcome. Among 408 patients, clinically significant PE was confirmed in 144 (35.3%) and any PE in 154 (37.7%). The Wells score demonstrated better discrimination for clinically significant PE than the simplified revised Geneva score (area under the curve 0.725 [95%CI: 0.671-0.779] vs 0.656 [95%CI: 0.598-0.714]; P = 0.0003). Clinically significant PE was present in 21.6% and 24.4% of patients classified as PE unlikely by the Wells and simplified revised Geneva two-level classifications, respectively. Among 398 patients with D-dimer results, YEARS and PEGeD each demonstrated 96.5% sensitivity but identified only 13.8% and 13.6% of patients, respectively, as potentially eligible for imaging avoidance. Diagnostic performance showed a similar pattern for any PE. In this CTPA-selected cohort, the Wells score demonstrated better discrimination than the simplified revised Geneva score, but both two-level classifications yielded substantial counterfactual missed-PE rates. YEARS and PEGeD maintained high sensitivity but offered limited theoretical imaging-sparing potential.

articles.title: Backcountry Risk-Taking (BRiT)-An Instrument to Evaluate an Individual's Overall Risk-Taking Behavior Within the Backcountry Avalanche Environment.
articles.abstract: Study HypothesisThe primary objective of this study was to develop and evaluate a novel instrument called the Backcountry Risk-Taking Instrument (BRiT) to measure risk-taking behavior among backcountry users. We aimed to create an instrument that is content-valid, grounded in theory, and psychometrically sound.MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study to evaluate the psychometric properties of the instrument. Participants completed the newly developed 13-item instrument along with established measures of risk-taking behavior and risk preference to assess convergent validity.ResultsA total of 361 participants completed the survey. After listwise deletion, n = 280 were retained for factor analysis and n = 354 for convergent validity. The resulting instrument provides a concise, empirically supported framework for measuring backcountry risk behavior and establishes a foundation for prospective validation in future cohorts.ConclusionsThe BRiT instrument significantly advances avalanche risk assessment. BRiT demonstrates a clear and stable foundation built upon 3 domains: Core Gear, Avalanche History, and Terrain Choice. Continued validation and refinement across broader populations will strengthen its utility as a foundational tool for both research and applied avalanche risk management.

articles.title: Ambient Heat Exposure Is Not Associated with Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction among Emergency Department Patients with Acute Chest Pain.
articles.abstract: BackgroundHeat exposure increases cardiovascular risk, but its relationship with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) in emergency department (ED) patients is unknown. This study examined whether heat exposure increases NSTEMI risk in ED patients with chest pain.MethodsThis observational cohort study of adults with chest pain from 5 US EDs (April 1, 2019-October 31, 2023) used the Wake Forest Chest Pain Registry. Heat data were collected from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Heat exposure was defined as maximum daily heat index ≥80°F, the National Weather Service's cautionary threshold. The primary outcome was index NSTEMI, determined using validated diagnosis codes. Logistic models assessed the association between heat and NSTEMI. Multivariable models were adjusted for common cardiovascular confounders, and pollution-given its potential to exacerbate cardiovascular disease. Lagged analysis evaluated heat exposure over 5-d lags. Unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios (aORs) are reported with 95% confidence intervals.ResultsAmong 21,367 patients with chest pain, 52.7% (11,260/21,367) were female, the median age was 53.5 y (IQR 40-65), and 63.1% (13,486/21,367) had heat-exposed days. Index NSTEMI occurred in 5.9% of patients. NSTEMI rates were similar between those with and without heat exposure (5.8% [778/13,486] vs 6.2% [487/7881]; OR: 0.93, 95% CI 0.83-1.05). After adjustment, heat exposure remained unassociated with index NSTEMI (aOR: 0.91, 95% CI 0.80-1.03). Lagged analysis showed no association between NSTEMI and heat exposure in unadjusted (OR: 0.92, 95% CI 0.82-1.04) or adjusted (aOR: 0.94, 95% CI 0.82-1.07) models.ConclusionHeat exposure was not associated with NSTEMI in chest pain ED patients.

articles.title: Comparing Internal Self-Assessment and External Evaluation of Hospital Safety Index (HSI) for Disaster Response: A Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract: Hospitals must ensure preparedness and safety to maintain services during disasters. Results from the Hospital Safety Index (HSI) often indicate that hospitals are safe and capable; however, it is important to verify whether these assessments are consistent across different evaluators. This study compared hospital safety scores between internal evaluators (hospital staff) and external evaluators. This cross-sectional study was conducted in 2022 using documented hospital safety assessment data from hospitals supervised by Kermanshah University of Medical Sciences (KUMS) in western Iran. Independent-samples t-tests, the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), and Bland-Altman plots were used to compare mean scores and assess agreement between evaluators. For structural safety, the difference between internal and external evaluators was not significant (95% CI, -9.19 to 9.67). In contrast, the differences were pronounced for non-structural safety (95% CI, 7.00 to 20.63) and functional safety (95% CI, 10.56 to 28.84), with both confidence intervals excluding zero. Agreement between evaluators was poor across most hospital safety domains (ICC < 0.05). Internal evaluators rated their hospitals significantly safer than external evaluators did. Given the pronounced differences in non-structural and functional safety, and the poor inter-rater agreement across most domains, relying solely on internal assessments may mislead hospital managers about disaster preparedness. Hospital managers should therefore regard external evaluation as an opportunity to reveal their hospital's vulnerabilities in disaster safety.

articles.title: Province-wide assessment of emergency care capacity and skills in a rural provincial health system: A facility-based cross-sectional assessment in Battambang, Cambodia.
articles.abstract: Emergency care capacity remains critically limited in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), particularly in rural areas where specialists and infrastructure are scarce. In Cambodia, stroke and ischemic heart disease are leading causes of mortality, and trauma burdens are increasing alongside rapid infrastructure development. Evidence on emergency equipment availability and frontline provider skills at the facility level in rural provinces remains limited. A facility-based cross-sectional assessment was conducted across all seven public referral hospitals in Battambang Province, Cambodia, in January 2023. Emergency equipment availability was evaluated through structured interviews and direct visual confirmation against the World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care. Clinical skill examinations were administered to physicians (two scenario-based cases: acute stroke with airway compromise; traumatic injury with tension pneumothorax and intra-abdominal bleeding) and nurses (a Basic Life Support [BLS] scenario assessed in pairs). Hospitals were stratified by Complementary Package of Activities (CPA) level: CPA1 (basic care only), CPA2 (including surgery and intensive care), and CPA3 (highest provincial level). At Complementary Package of Activities (CPA)1 (basic care only) hospitals, intubation equipment and 12-lead electrocardiogram were each available in only 25% of facilities. None had a crash cart, blood transfusion capacity, basic metabolic panel, or coagulation testing. In the stroke scenario, airway patency was confirmed by 28.6% of physicians at CPA1 hospitals, compared with 70.0% at CPA2 hospitals (including surgery and intensive care), 57.1% at the CPA3 hospital (highest provincial level), and 75.0% at the Provincial Health Department. In the trauma scenario, no physician at CPA1 hospitals correctly performed spinal immobilization with the spine kept straight or thoracentesis at the correct anatomical location. Among 38 nurse pairs, 97.4% initiated chest compressions promptly, but only 21.1% demonstrated correct compression technique, and 13.2% provided effective bag-valve-mask ventilation. Deficiencies in equipment and clinical skills were most pronounced at CPA1 hospitals. Emergency care capacity in Battambang Province was substantially limited, with the greatest deficiencies at CPA1 hospitals. Recurrent low-cost training and targeted strengthening of basic emergency care should be prioritized at lower-level facilities.

articles.title: Letter: Radiocarpal stability in chronic radiocarpal dislocation: Osteotomy is only one part of reconstruction.
Addition of a McLaughlin cerclage to locking plate fixation of distal patellar pole fractures reduces interfragmentary displacement - a biomechanical human cadaveric study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: To investigate whether the addition of a McLaughlin cerclage to locking plate fixation of distal patellar pole fractures provides improved biomechanical construct stability and reduced interfragmentary displacement. A distal patellar pole fracture was simulated in sixteen fresh-frozen human cadaveric knees by a horizontal osteotomy in the distal third of the patella. Subsequently, locking plate fixation was performed. In a randomized half of the specimens, an additional McLaughlin wire cerclage was applied. The specimens were then subjected to 3000 cycles of extension starting at 90° of flexion under a maximum tensile load of 320 N. Using a Digital Image Correlation (DIC) system, the interfragmentary displacement between the proximal and distal fragments was measured at 1, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 2000, and 3000 cycles. Statistical analysis was performed using repeated-measures ANOVA and Welch's unpaired t-t test at 3000 cycles. An additional McLaughlin cerclage significantly reduced interfragmentary displacement under cyclic loading in comparison to locking plate fixation alone. After 3000 cycles, displacement was 2.27 ± 1.84 mm with plate fixation alone and 0.36 ± 0.22 mm with additional McLaughlin cerclage (mean difference 1.91 mm; 95% CI 0.38-3.45 mm; p = 0.0215). An additional McLaughlin cerclage reduced interfragmentary displacement in distal patellar pole fractures. In cases of unstable distal pole patella fractures, the additional use of a McLaughlin cerclage may therefore be considered to enhance construct stability.

articles.title: Trauma care performance and patient outcomes - insights from a major trauma centre in Sweden.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Trauma is a leading cause of death among individuals under 45 years of age. Evaluating trauma system performance over time is important but inherently difficult due to concurrent changes in patient demographics, case-mix and care processes. The aim of this study was to describe temporal changes in patient demographics, injury severity and trauma care at a major trauma centre in Sweden from 2017 to 2023. We hypothesised that risk-adjusted 30-day mortality decreased and that time to computed tomography was reduced over the study period. A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from the Karolinska Trauma Registry, including all trauma patients aged > 15 years fulfilling criteria for full trauma team activation, admitted between January 2017 and August 2023. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess changes in 30-day mortality over time, adjusted for age, sex, injury severity category, ASA score and injury type. Time from arrival to computed tomography was analysed by linear regression and, because the distribution was skewed, by quantile (median) regression. A total of 5,615 trauma patients were included. Over the study period, the patient population became older, and ASA scores increased, while injury severity and the proportion of penetrating injury remained unchanged. In multivariable logistic regression with 2017 as reference, the odds of 30-day mortality in 2022-2023 were lower (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.43-0.88, P = 0.008) after adjusting for confounders. Median time to computed tomography decreased from 31 to 21 min; the adjusted difference in 2022-2023 compared with 2017 was - 7.5 min by linear regression (P = 0.014) and - 10.4 min by quantile regression (95% CI - 11.5 to - 9.2, P < 0.001). Our findings are consistent with improvements in trauma care within a mature trauma system, with shorter median time to computed tomography and lower 30-day mortality despite an aging population with increasing comorbidity. However, the specific drivers of these changes are difficult to identify, and future studies should explore how individual components of pre-hospital and in-hospital care contribute to trauma outcomes.

articles.title: Quantifying Biomechanical Demand During Manual Overboard Rescue: Scenario-Based Application of the Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation.
articles.abstract: BackgroundMaritime first responders frequently perform manual overboard lifting during rescue operations, placing them at high risk for musculoskeletal injury, particularly in the lumbar spine. Conventional ergonomic guidelines, including the Revised National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) Lifting Equation (RNLE), were developed for controlled, symmetrical lifting and do not adequately capture the biomechanical and environmental demands of overboard recovery.PurposeThis study aimed to quantify biomechanical demand during overboard lifting from vessels with 1.8- to 3.0-m freeboard and to evaluate injury risk under conditions exceeding standard RNLE assumptions.MethodsThe RNLE was adapted to estimate Recommended Weight Limit (RWL) and Lifting Index (LI) for overboard lifting tasks. Scenario-based analyses examined object masses (0-140 kg), horizontal reaches (25-50 cm), and vertical lifting distances (0-175 cm). LI values were calculated at both lift origin and destination to capture phase-specific biomechanical risk.ResultsUnder idealized conditions, LI exceeded the recommended safety threshold (LI > 1) at loads as low as 15.6 kg for a horizontal reach of 25 cm. For a human-sized load of 90 kg, LI ranged from 3.9 to 7.8 depending on horizontal reach and vertical displacement, indicating substantial biomechanical overload. Increasing horizontal reach from 25 to 50 cm increased LI by 40 to 60% across all load conditions. LI exceeded 1 at both the lift origin and destination for all modeled loads ≥20 kg and vertical displacements ≥50 cm, highlighting the elevated risk inherent in these tasks.ConclusionManual overboard lifting imposes significant biomechanical strain that frequently exceeds conventional ergonomic limits. Task-specific metrics derived here provide quantitative guidance for injury prevention, including pre-employment functional screening, progressive task-specific conditioning, and the use of mechanical assistive devices. These findings support evidence-based occupational health strategies for maritime first responders and other personnel performing high-risk lifting tasks in dynamic environments.

articles.title: The Continuing Evolution of the International Diploma in Mountain Medicine: Balancing Global Standards and Local Context.
Physiological monitoring and physiology-informed strategies in cardiac arrest: current evidence and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Despite advances in cardiac arrest management, survival with favorable neurological outcomes remains limited. Physiological monitoring may complement standardized resuscitation by providing real-time information about circulatory effectiveness, reversible causes, and treatment responses. However, whether physiology-guided interventions improve patient-centered outcomes remains uncertain. This narrative review examines the current evidence and clinical applicability of physiological monitoring during resuscitation, physiology-informed rescue strategies, and individualized post-cardiac arrest care. During cardiopulmonary resuscitation, invasive arterial pressure monitoring, waveform capnography, and echocardiography provide complementary information about the circulation generated by chest compressions and potential mechanisms of resuscitation failure. Although observational and experimental studies support their physiological relevance, no adult diastolic pressure target or pressure-guided vasopressor strategy has been validated to improve survival or neurological recovery. Recent randomized trials of transesophageal echocardiography have demonstrated physiological or procedural effects without establishing clinical benefit. Among rescue strategies, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation has yielded inconsistent results across randomized trials, with potential benefits dependent on patient selection, intervention timing, and system capabilities. Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta has not improved clinical outcomes in randomized evaluation, while head-up resuscitation remains investigational. Following the return of spontaneous circulation, randomized trials have challenged the benefits of uniformly higher blood pressure and oxygenation targets, mild hypercapnia, and deeper or prolonged temperature control. Individualized approaches incorporating cerebral autoregulation, venous congestion, and cardiopulmonary physiology are physiologically appealing but lack prospective validation. Physiological assessment may complement established resuscitation algorithms by refining clinical decisions during and after cardiac arrest. However, improvements in physiological measurements should not be equated with improved patient outcomes. Future trials should determine whether predefined, physiology-guided treatment strategies improve survival and neurological recovery.

articles.title: Phenotyping of Arrhythmia-induced Cardiomyopathy: From Bench to Bedside and Back.
articles.abstract: Arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy (AIC) is an increasingly recognized and potentially reversible cause or modifier of heart failure. This review summarizes experimental and clinical evidence with a focus on atrial fibrillation (AFib)-induced left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Recent studies demonstrate that AIC extends beyond tachycardia alone and involves rhythm irregularity, loss of atrioventricular synchrony, altered calcium handling, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and substrate vulnerability. Clinical trials demonstrate the superiority of rhythm control therapy by catheter ablation in patients with AFib and heart failure. Emerging data illustrate the importance of phenotyping of AIC according to myocardial substrate and individual ventricular response to AFib. AIC should be considered as a heterogeneous spectrum. Refined phenotyping may improve prediction of recovery and guide specific and individual therapy.

articles.title: Don't Wait- Ablate! Catheter Ablation in Patients with Advanced Heart Failure and Atrial Fibrillation.
articles.abstract: Heart failure (HF) and atrial fibrillation (AF) frequently coexist and mutually accelerate disease progression through complex hemodynamic, neurohormonal, and structural interactions. Although earlier rhythm-control strategies failed to demonstrate mortality benefit, largely due to limitations of antiarrhythmic drug therapy, catheter ablation has fundamentally altered the therapeutic landscape. The CASTLE-AF trial established catheter ablation as a disease-modifying therapy in patients with AF and HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), demonstrating reductions in mortality and HF hospitalization. More recently, the CASTLE-HTx trial extended these findings to patients with end-stage HF eligible for heart transplantation (HTx) or left ventricular assist device (LVAD) therapy. Catheter ablation has demonstrated a marked reduction in mortality and the need of an urgent HTx, or LVAD implantation compared with medical therapy alone. Subsequent subanalyses further refined risk stratification and identified patient subsets deriving the greatest benefit. Therefore, catheter ablation has received a class 1 recommendation for patients with AF and HFrEF. According to recent clinical evidence supporting early rhythm control through catheter ablation in advanced HF, it leads to a paradigm shift in the management of this high-risk population: in selected patients with AF and advanced HF, clinicians should not delay referral-"Don't wait, ablate."

articles.title: From physical healing to psychological readiness: Integrating virtual reality-based CBT into post-crash rehabilitation.
articles.abstract: This Letter to the Editor responds to Erdogan-Yildirim et al.'s review on the psychological and behavioral consequences of physical injuries after road traffic crashes. While the review highlights posttraumatic stress symptoms, driving-related avoidance, trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, and virtual reality-based exposure, the operational integration of these components into post-crash rehabilitation requires further clarification. The novelty of this perspective lies in reframing recovery as a staged transition from physical healing to psychological readiness. We propose that virtual reality-based CBT may reduce post-crash psychological distress by modifying catastrophic driving-related appraisals, decreasing avoidance behavior, and strengthening driving self-efficacy through graded, therapist-guided driving simulations. This approach could be embedded after medical stabilization through early psychological screening, brief CBT, controlled virtual exposure, and gradual return-to-mobility planning. Future studies should test whether reduced driving avoidance and improved self-efficacy mediate psychological recovery after road traffic crashes.

articles.title: From missed injury to overdiagnosis.
Early fecal diversion versus no initial diversion in blunt open pelvic fractures: A systematic review and meta-analysis of pelvic infection and mortality.
articles.abstract: The benefit of routine early fecal diversion in blunt open pelvic fractures remains uncertain. We examined its association with pelvic infection and short-term mortality. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and CENTRAL were searched from inception through 12 August 2026, with citation searching. Comparative observational studies were synthesized using crude risk ratios (RRs), REML random-effects models, modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals, and Mantel-Haenszel sensitivity analyses without continuity correction. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed ROBINS-I risk of bias and GRADE certainty. Eighteen observational comparative reports were retained. Potential cohort overlap prevented a valid unique overall participant total. Eight cohorts contributed to broad pelvic infection (171 participants; seven estimable): RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.35-1.70; I²=19.6%). The stricter outcome-definition analysis included five cohorts (88 participants; four estimable): RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.07-6.97). Excluding two author-reported infected hematomas through an existing replacement sensitivity gave RR 0.84 (95% CI 0.34-2.05). Eight mortality cohorts (236 participants) yielded RR 0.82 (95% CI 0.33-2.07; I²=19.0%). Post-2006 evidence remained inconclusive for infection (three cohorts; RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.009-58.85) and mortality (five cohorts; RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.27-5.26). Diversion was preferentially used in patients with more severe injuries. All reports had Serious or Critical risk of bias; certainty was very low. Available evidence does not establish a reduction in pelvic infection or short-term mortality with routine early diversion. Confounding, inconsistent outcome ascertainment, and imprecision prevent causal conclusions or exclusion of benefit in selected high-risk injuries.

articles.title: Corrigendum to "Proximal humerus fractures: A review of current management evidence and guidance on contemporary surgical strategies" [Injury 57(11) (2026) 113748].
Chest tube fixation strength depends on suture caliber and fixation technique rather than tube diameter: a biomechanical cadaver study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Chest tube dislodgement remains a relevant complication in emergency, trauma, and intensive care medicine. In a previous biomechanical study, the Modified Johannesburg technique using Mersilene USP 1 demonstrated superior fixation strength compared with other chest tube fixation techniques. The present study aimed to determine whether suture size, suture material, and chest tube diameter influence fixation strength. A prospective interventional biomechanical cadaveric study was performed using fresh porcine thoracic wall specimens. A total of 320 load-to-failure tests were conducted under standardized laboratory conditions. Two fixation techniques, Modified Johannesburg and Purse String, were compared using two chest tube diameters (20/28 Ch) and four non-absorbable braided suture configurations: Mersilene USP 1, Mersilene USP 2 - 0, Silk USP 1, and Silk USP 2 - 0. Each experimental group consisted of 20 specimens. Specimens were tested in a uniaxial testing machine until construct failure. Force [N] and elongation [mm] at failure were measured. The experiments were videotaped, and the failure mechanism was analyzed. The Modified Johannesburg technique demonstrated significantly higher pull-out forces compared to the Purse String technique (125.0 vs. 66.4 N; p < 0.001), as did larger suture sizes (USP 1 vs. 2 - 0; p < 0.001) and Mersilene compared to Silk (114.6 vs. 76.9 N; p < 0.001). Chest tube size had only a very small and inconsistent effect on pull-out strength. The predominant failure mode was suture rupture (94.7%). Chest tube fixation strength is significantly influenced by fixation technique, suture size, and suture material. The effect of chest tube diameter on fixation strength appeared negligible. The Modified Johannesburg technique, size 1 sutures, and Mersilene material provided superior biomechanical stability. Since failure occurred predominantly by suture rupture, the suture appears to represent the weakest link of the fixation construct.

articles.title: Changes in patellar height following suprapatellar and infrapatellar tibial nailing: a retrospective comparative cohort study.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Patella baja has been described after infrapatellar tibial nailing and may contribute to postoperative knee morbidity; however, whether the nail insertion approach influences postoperative patellar height remains unclear. This study compared longitudinal changes in patellar height (PH) after suprapatellar and infrapatellar intramedullary nailing for tibial shaft fractures. We hypothesized that the suprapatellar approach would better preserve patellar height. A retrospective comparative cohort study included 114 tibial shaft fractures treated with intramedullary nailing between 2016 and 2023, using a suprapatellar (n = 86) or infrapatellar (n = 28) approach. Patellar height was assessed using the Caton-Deschamps Index (CDI) on preoperative and final follow-up radiographs. The primary outcome was the longitudinal change in CDI (ΔCDI). Fracture union, complications, and reoperations were secondary outcomes. The mean reduction in CDI was greater following infrapatellar than suprapatellar nailing (ΔCDI - 0.116 ± 0.173 vs. -0.011 ± 0.107; p = 0.001). After adjustment for baseline CDI and follow-up duration, this association remained significant (adjusted β=-0.055; 95% CI - 0.107 to - 0.004; p = 0.035), although sensitivity analyses showed attenuation after additional adjustment for sex. Fracture union rates were similar between approaches (93.0% vs. 92.9%; p = 0.987), with no statistically significant differences in complications or reoperations. Infrapatellar tibial nailing was associated with a significant postoperative reduction in PH compared with the suprapatellar approach. This association persisted after adjustment for baseline CDI and follow-up duration but was sensitive to additional adjustment for sex. These findings highlight a potential relationship between nail insertion approach and postoperative PH but do not establish an independent effect of surgical approach. Retrospective cohort study (Level III).

articles.title: Intraarticular calcaneal fractures: biomechanical analysis of two fixation constructs.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: The aim of this biomechanical study was to investigate the fixation stability of a small low-profile 2.7 mm variable-angle locking anterolateral calcaneal plate supplemented with two additional independent cortex screws versus a traditional small 3.5 mm locking calcaneal plate in a standardized Sanders IIc fracture model. Sixteen fracture models cocomposed of three polymer blocks (fragments) each and simulating Sanders IIc intra‑articular calcaneal fractures were assigned to two groups. Group 1 (control) received a small 3.5 mm locking calcaneal plate, while Group 2 received a small 2.7 mm variable‑angle locking anterolateral calcaneal plate with two additional independent cortex screws. All constructs were instrumented using prefabricated pilot holes and standardized screw configurations. Biomechanical testing was conducted implementing a 3‑point-bending setup and progressively increasing cyclic loading to failure. Angular interfragmentary movements were quantified via motion tracking along with cycles to clinically relevant failure. Initial stiffness (N/mm) in Group 1 (65.2 ± 34.7) was significantly lower versus Group 2 (232.5 ± 48.6), p = 0.020. Although angular interfragmentary movements around the anteroposterior axis were significantly greater in Group 1 versus Group 2 (p < 0.001), Group 1 demonstrated significantly smaller angular interfragmentary movements around the mediolateral axis for the central-to-posterior and anterior-to-posterior fragment pairs (p ≤ 0.004), while no significant difference between the groups was identified with regard to the central-to-anterior fragment pair (p ≥ 0.377). Cycles and loads (N) to clinically relevant failure in Group 1 (3635 ± 176 and 92.7 ± 3.5) were significantly lower versus Group 2 (17433 ± 628 and 368.7 ± 12.6), p < 0.001. Failure mode in Group 1 involved plate deformation, whereas Group 2 failed through breakage or bending of the independent cortex screws. Biomechanically, fixation implementing a small low-profile 2.7 mm variable-angle locking anterolateral calcaneal plate supplemented with two additional independent cortex screws demonstrated stability comparable to, and in certain respects superior to that achieved with a small 3.5 mm locking calcaneal plate in a standardized Sanders IIc fracture model. However, the findings of this laboratory study do not establish an isolated benefit of the 2.7 mm plate itself, nor do they demonstrate clinical superiority or support alterations to postoperative weight-bearing protocols.

articles.title: Correction: Time to surgery and its impact on length of stay and mortality for neck of femur fractures at a major trauma centre.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society

articles.title: Demographic Data Concordance: A Prospective Observational Study of Adolescents, Caregivers, and the Electronic Health Record.
articles.abstract: (1) To measure the concordance of patient demographic data in the electronic health record (EHR); and (2) to determine the level of agreement for patient demographic data between patient report-EHR and patients-caregivers. We conducted a prospective observational survey of 295 patients (age 12 to 17 years) and caregiver dyads presenting to a pediatric emergency department. The primary outcome was concordance, reporting kappa statistics with 95% CI, of caregiver-reported patient race, ethnicity, and sex and the EHR. Secondary outcomes were concordance between: (1) patient report and EHR and (2) patient and caregiver report, including gender identity and preferred language. We surveyed dyads on the perceived impact of demographic characteristics on emergency care and caregivers on preferences for reporting data. For caregiver and EHR report of race, there was substantial agreement for Asian (κ=0.65, 95% CI: 0.44-0.86), Black/African American/African (κ=0.76, 95% CI: 0.66-0.86), and White (κ=0.66, 95% CI: 0.58-0.75) race and moderate agreement for Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (κ=0.53, 95% CI: 0.44-0.61). Patient report and the EHR had similar concordance for race and poor agreement for Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (κ=-0.17, 95% CI: -0.22 to -0.12). For patients and caregivers, there was strong concordance for race, ethnicity, language, and gender identity. Caregivers were more likely than pediatric patients to report that demographic factors affected emergency care. Most caregivers did not have preferences about demographic data reporting methods. Concordance of patient race and ethnicity data in the EHR was variable and should be interpreted cautiously.

articles.title: What Does High F1 Mean in LLM-Based Pediatric Pneumonia Classification?

Enhanced wound healing potential of a carboxymethyl cellulose/gelatin-based hydrogel containing decellularized amniotic membrane and Matricaria chamomilla extract: A multifunctional composite dressing.
articles.abstract: Chronic wound healing remains a complex biological process influenced by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, microbial invasion, and insufficient tissue regeneration. Therefore, the design of multifunctional biomaterials that integrate structural support with biological regulation has emerged as a promising strategy in advanced wound care. This study sought to develop a composite hydrogel incorporating decellularized amniotic membrane (dAM)-derived extracellular matrix components alongside Matricaria chamomilla extract, with the goal of achieving enhanced regenerative and therapeutic outcomes. A CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM hydrogel was prepared using decellularized dAM and subsequently evaluated in terms of its physicochemical and biological characteristics. The effectiveness of the decellularization process and preservation of ECM components were first examined, followed by characterization of hydrogel morphology, rheological properties, swelling and degradation behavior, and pH stability. Its biological performance was further assessed through hemocompatibility, cytocompatibility, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial assays, as well as a full-thickness wound model. Incorporation of dAM and chamomile extract resulted in a stable hydrogel with favorable physicochemical and biological characteristics. The decellularization procedure removed 97.9% of the DNA. The resulting composite hydrogel exhibited an average pore size of 78.3 ± 9.8 µm, and all hydrogel formulations showed hemolysis rates below the 5% threshold accepted for blood-contacting biomaterials, with values ranging from 3.8% to 4.5%. The composite hydrogel also supported enhanced fibroblast viability (109.6 ± 11.3%) and demonstrated antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial activities against wound-associated pathogens. In vivo, treatment with CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM accelerated wound closure (85.7 ± 6.3% at day 14) and supported tissue regeneration, outperforming both the dAM-containing hydrogel (78.9 ± 9.9%) and the commercial DuoDERM dressing (58.9 ± 4.5%), as evidenced by improved re-epithelialization, collagen deposition, angiogenesis, and early signs of tissue remodeling. The CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM hydrogel combines a dAM-containing extracellular matrix scaffold with chamomile-derived bioactive compounds, creating a favorable microenvironment for tissue repair. The addition of chamomile extract to the dAM-containing scaffold was associated with improved wound closure and tissue regeneration. While the present study design does not permit a definitive assessment of synergy between dAM and chamomile, these findings support the potential of this formulation as a multifunctional biomaterial platform for advanced wound healing applications.

articles.title: Can Emergency Physicians Identify Frozen Tissue on Ultrasound? Implications for Frostbite Management.
articles.abstract: IntroductionFrostbite injuries cause disfigurement and loss of functionality. The role of early imaging in management remains unclear because most modalities require infrastructure that prevents field application. Providers use point-of-care ultrasound to assess a range of soft tissue and musculoskeletal pathologies. The primary objective of this study is to determine the accuracy with which emergency physicians can identify frozen tissue on ultrasound.MethodsThree emergency medicine physicians evaluated whether porcine tissue was frozen or unfrozen by viewing standardized ultrasound clips. The team recorded clips of tissue thawing in a water bath from -10 to +10°C using a handheld ultrasound device. Each physician independently reviewed randomized clips and recorded their assessments. A 2 × 2 table was used to calculate the pooled sensitivity and specificity.ResultsEmergency medicine physicians reviewed 75 clips. They achieved a pooled sensitivity of 76% (95% CI 0.60-0.87) and a specificity of 87% (95% CI 0.68-0.96) for detecting frozen tissue compared with the tissue thermometer as the standard. Their results showed an overall accuracy of 80% (95% CI 0.69-0.88).ConclusionsIn this pilot study, emergency medicine physicians with advanced point-of-care ultrasound training identified frozen tissue on ultrasound 80% of the time. Future research should explore the sonographic features of frozen tissue in cases of frostbite and the test characteristics for sonographers with varying skill levels.

articles.title: Flight Physician Training and Workforce Sustainability Within an Integrated Emergency Department-Intensive Care Unit-Helicopter Emergency Medical Services Staffing Model: A Rural Helicopter Emergency Medical Services Experience in Japan.
articles.abstract: Maintaining physician-staffed helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS) in rural regions is increasingly challenging because of physician shortages, workforce sustainability concerns, and limited opportunities for dedicated flight physician staffing. We developed an integrated staffing and training model in which emergency physicians collectively provide emergency department (ED), intensive care unit (ICU), pediatric emergency, and HEMS care while participating in a regional physician-sharing collaboration. This single-center retrospective study evaluated all consecutive HEMS missions conducted between April 2021 and March 2026 at a rural tertiary emergency and critical care center in Japan. Flight physician training was conducted through on-the-job training (OJT) embedded within routine ED, ICU, pediatric emergency, and HEMS practices. Missions performed during supervised OJT were compared with those performed after independent certification. Operational performance was assessed using on-scene time, scene intervention rates, intubation rates, cardiopulmonary resuscitation rates, and hospital mortality. Six physicians completed training; 4 achieved independent practice within 6 months and 2 within 12 months. The average annual flight volume was approximately 30 missions per physician. A total of 189 missions were analyzed. Patient characteristics were comparable between 98 OJT and 91 independent missions. No differences were observed across operational performance measures; no procedural, medication, or operational incidents occurred. Despite relatively limited individual flight exposure, most trainees achieved independent practice within 6 months, and operational performance following certification was not inferior to that of supervised training. Integrated acute care practice may support the development and maintenance of flight physician competency in resource-limited rural environments.

articles.title: The Operational Impact of a Tertiary Hospital Heliport in Lisbon: A One‑Year Operational Review.
articles.abstract: Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) are a key component of modern emergency and critical care systems, improving access to time‑sensitive interventions for critically ill patients. In Portugal, the certification and reopening of the Santa Maria Hospital Heliport (SMHH) in March 2025 established a continuously 24/7 hospital heliport in Lisbon. To describe the first year of operation of the SMHH and evaluate its role in national aeromedical connectivity and patient redistribution within a metropolitan hospital network. A retrospective descriptive study was conducted including all helicopter movements recorded at the SMHH between March 2025 and March 2026, using the institutional operational registry. Variables included number of landings, temporal distribution, mission type and final destination. During the first year of operation, a total of 235 landings were recorded. Primary HEMS mission accounted for approximately 60% of all operations, followed by secondary inter-hospital transfers (35%) and specialized ECMO and organ missions (5%). Less than 10% of helicopter missions to the Lisbon metropolitan area required diversion to alternative certified heliports. The implementation of a certified 24/7 hospital heliport established an effective aeromedical hub for the Lisbon metropolitan area, faciliting direct helicopter acces and coordinated distribution of patients to the most appropriate referral hospitals, while potentially reducing the need for secondary ground transfers. Further studies are required to quantify its impact on transfer times and patient outcomes.

articles.title: REBOAHEMS: A Standardized, Competency-Based Operational Training Model for Air Medical REBOA Implementation.
articles.abstract: Massive hemorrhage remains a leading cause of preventable trauma mortality. Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) has been proposed as a potential prehospital intervention, including within helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS). However, safe REBOA implementation in air medical environments poses unique operational challenges, and training models specifically adapted to these conditions remain scarce. The objective of this study is to develop and evaluate the operational feasibility of a structured training program designed to prepare HEMS crews for REBOA implementation under real air medical constraints. REBOAHEMS was designed as a competency-based, blended-learning program consisting of a 12-hour online phase and a 12-hour in-person high-contextual-fidelity simulation phase conducted in helicopter cabin simulators (Bell 412 and AW109). A prospective educational evaluation was performed in HEMS physicians and nurses, assessing knowledge acquisition (pre-/post-test), procedural performance in simulation (Objective Structured Assessment of Prehospital REBOA Application scores and time to aortic occlusion), participant satisfaction, and early indicators of perceived transfer to clinical practice. A total of 14 HEMS clinicians completed the program. Participants demonstrated significant improvement in theoretical knowledge and consistent procedural performance during simulated air medical scenarios. The mean time to aortic occlusion was 9.0 ± 3.6 minutes. Overall satisfaction was high. Although participants reported increased identification of potential REBOA candidates after training, no clinical REBOA deployments occurred due to a lack of device availability. REBOAHEMS represents a feasible approach to preparing HEMS crews for REBOA performance under air medical operational constraints. The findings highlight that training alone is insufficient for clinical implementation, emphasizing the critical role of organizational readiness, equipment availability, and governance structures. This model offers a reproducible framework for air medical programs seeking to safely advance REBOA readiness and implementation.

articles.title: Peer Support for a Specialty Critical Care Transport Team.
articles.abstract: First responders experience higher rates of psychological distress than the general population, driven by repeated exposure to traumatic events and limited recovery time. Members of neonatal and pediatric critical care transport teams face additional cumulative stressors related to high-acuity patients and emotionally challenging transports. This study describes the development, implementation, and utilization of a peer-led support program within a hospital-based neonatal and pediatric critical care transport service. Following a 2019 internal survey that identified a preference for peer-based emotional support, the Children's Mercy Critical Care Transport Team implemented a structured peer support program. Peer Support Persons (PSPs) were selected from a multidisciplinary transport team and completed standardized initial and ongoing training. Peer support was accessed through self-referral, leadership referral, and a confidential QR code (Quick Response Code) request system. Minimal, non-identifiable encounter data were tracked in a secure database. Descriptive analysis was used to evaluate program utilization from March 2023 to August 2025. During the study period, 209 peer support encounters were documented, including 11 formal debriefings and 199 informal interactions. Encounters involved registered nurses, respiratory therapists, emergency medical technicians, communication specialists, and other team members, most of which were related to difficult transports, patient deaths, and emotional distress. Program utilization increased over time, demonstrating the integration of peer support into routine team culture. Staff feedback was consistently positive, highlighting the value of timely, confidential, peer-led support. A structured, confidential, peer-led support program is feasible and sustainable in a neonatal and pediatric critical care transport setting. This model promotes resilience, reduces stigma, and may serve as a framework for similar first-responder programs.

articles.title: Helicopter and Fixed-Wing Air Medical Transport in a Resource-Limited Region of Eastern Anatolia: Epidemiological Patterns and Operational Challenges in Van Province, Turkey (2022-2025).
articles.abstract: Air ambulance services are essential for patient transport in geographically isolated and resource-limited regions. Van Province, located in the easternmost part of Turkey, features mountainous terrain, harsh winters, and frequent road closures. Despite the critical role of air medical transport in such challenging environments, epidemiological data from these regions remain scarce. This study aimed to characterize the distinct operational roles, patient demographics, and clinical indications for helicopter versus fixed-wing air ambulance transport in a geographically challenging, resource-limited region. We conducted a retrospective, descriptive epidemiological study analyzing all air ambulance transports (n = 940) coordinated by the Van Provincial Emergency Medical Services between January 1, 2022, and December 31, 2025. Demographic, clinical, and operational data were compared between helicopter and fixed-wing transports. To address the well-known limitation that the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is not interpretable in patients who are pharmacologically sedated or intubated, the primary GCS comparison was performed in a subset of 738 patients after excluding 190 patients who were intubated, mechanically ventilated, or sedated at the time of preflight assessment; the excluded group is described separately. Of 940 patients, 537 (57.1%) were transported by helicopter and 403 (42.9%) by fixed-wing aircraft. Helicopter patients were significantly older (38.4 vs. 18.4 years, P < .001) and predominantly adults (70.9%). Fixed-wing aircraft primarily transported neonates and children (71.0%), particularly those with congenital heart disease (n = 147, 92.5% fixed-wing). After excluding patients who were intubated, mechanically ventilated, or sedated (n = 190), mean preflight GCS was 14.7 ± 1.4 in the helicopter group versus 14.2 ± 1.6 in the fixed-wing group (P < .001); although this difference was statistically significant, the magnitude of this difference is unlikely to be clinically meaningful, as both groups were essentially alert. The geographically isolated Bahçesaray district accounted for 295 patients (31.4%), all of whom were transported by helicopter. All 52 scene responses were performed exclusively by helicopters. Helicopter and fixed-wing aircraft serve distinct and complementary roles in the air medical system of eastern Turkey. These findings provide an operational reference for resource-limited regions and underscore the need for outcome-linked research to evaluate clinical effectiveness.

articles.title: International Fixed-Wing Air Ambulance Repatriation: A Retrospective Observational Cohort Analysis With Regression Modeling of Fox Flight Air Ambulance Inc. Patient Repatriation Characteristics 2009 to 2024.
articles.abstract: As international travel rises globally, particularly among older adults with chronic conditions, illness or injury abroad may require air medical repatriation. Contemporary data describing patient characteristics, transport practices, and in-flight events are limited. The objective of this study is to describe the patient demographics, clinical indications, transport characteristics, and in-flight events associated with international fixed-wing air medical repatriation by a single Canadian provider. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of all international repatriations completed by Fox Flight Air Ambulance Inc. between 2009 and 2024. Extracted chart data included demographics, diagnoses, transport modality, team composition, interventions, and in-flight events. Outcomes included repatriation completion, mortality, and in-flight events that required intervention. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with in-flight events. A total of 3,905 transports were included. Patients were predominantly older adults (61.5 ± 21.5 years), with orthopedic/trauma, cardiovascular, neurovascular, and infectious disease diagnoses comprising most repatriations. In-flight events occurred in 26.7% of transports; major events represented 15.0% of all events (3.9% of transports). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant associations (P < .001) between in-flight interventions and mechanical ventilation, team composition, age group, and transport era. Over time, patients required stretchers and oxygen therapy more frequently, consistent with increasing acuity. In multivariable analysis, independent predictors of in-flight events included age, orthopedic/trauma and neoplasm-related diagnoses, oxygen therapy, invasive mechanical ventilation, and year of transport. Serious in-flight events were infrequent and occurred within transports staffed by experienced teams, although causality cannot be inferred. The findings support risk-informed planning, team composition decisions, and operational strategies to optimize safety and resource utilization.

articles.title: Fatigue Characteristics and Perceptions in US Helicopter Air Ambulance Pilots.
articles.abstract: Helicopter air ambulance (HAA) operations involve shiftwork schedules that put personnel at an increased risk of fatigue. This survey study aimed to provide an updated benchmark for fatigue characteristics and perceptions within US HAA pilots. Pilots across the US HAA industry were invited to complete a survey related to their work and individual sleep-related preferences. Pilots completed the survey, including standardized questionnaires such as the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire, the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, during a larger field study. Our survey of 120 pilots across 21 operators revealed that poor self-reported sleep quality is an issue in more than half (53%) of the sample population. Most participants (71%) felt that fatigue was most prevalent on the return-to-base leg of a trip, and 69% felt that the number of flight requests was the greatest schedule-related contributor to fatigue. One-third of the pilots (34%) reported "nodding off" during a flight, and more than three-quarters (87%) said that their work performance had been affected by sleep inertia. The pilots provided suggestions as to how to mitigate fatigue risk through flight request limits, duty duration maximums, and sleep inertia protections. Overall, the results of this survey can be used to identify areas of fatigue risk to be addressed through operational policies and to highlight areas in need of further research.

articles.title: Forum November/ December- Air Medical Journal (YMAM).
Beyond Patient Acuity: Clinician Cognition and System Capability in Interfacility Helicopter Air Ambulance Utilization.
Using Checklists to Improve Turnaround Times in Time-Critical Interhospital Transfers.
articles.abstract: Time-critical interhospital transfer is operationally and clinically high-stake. Variation in referring-hospital preparation can prolong in-hospital turnaround time and delay definitive care. In 2022, time-critical interhospital transfers accounted for 1.5% of cases attended by a UK Helicopter Emergency Medicine Service (HEMS) organisation. Twenty-three patients were transferred, including 3 children. Our key performance indicator (KPI) of hospital turnaround time being less than 45 minutes was achieved in only 12 transfers (52%). A UK HEMS organisation that undertakes time-critical interhospital transfers from district general hospitals to regional tertiary centers. Two checklists (referring-team "Pre-arrival" and transport-team "Pre-departure") were developed. High-fidelity simulated time-critical transfer scenarios were undertaken in a simulation suite to improve crew familiarity before their introduction. The checklists were introduced into operational practice, and a post-intervention retrospective service evaluation of all interhospital helicopter transfers between January 1, 2024 and December 31, 2024 was then performed using routinely collected operational data (turnaround defined as landing-to-departure time at the referring hospital). In simulated scenarios, the < 45-minute turnaround KPI was consistently achieved. In 2024, after the introduction of the checklists, 11 interhospital transfers were completed by air (2 paediatric), representing 0.6% of all missions. The < 45-minute turnaround KPI was achieved in 7 (64%) time-critical transfers. Fisher exact test showed that the difference in KPI achievement did not reach statistical significance. Checklist-supported preparation may improve the reliability of meeting time-critical transfer KPIs while maintaining safe transfer standards. Owing to the relatively rare occurrence of these transfers, the absence of statistical significance should not be interpreted as an absence of a clinically meaningful effect. In routine practice, performance was influenced by outlier delays, suggesting a focus on reducing variability and embedding consistent pre-arrival preparation at referring sites.

articles.title: Feasibility of Prehospital Central Venous Cannulation During Cardiac Arrest in an Ambulance.
articles.abstract: Central venous cannulation is routinely performed in hospital settings but is rarely considered in the prehospital environment, where confined workspaces and concurrent resuscitative demands may limit procedural feasibility. We conducted a simulation-based feasibility study to evaluate whether central venous cannulation could be performed during ongoing cardiac arrest resuscitation within a standard ambulance. A multidisciplinary team consisting of emergency medical services clinicians and a physician participated in repeated simulations using a resuscitation manikin. A refractory shockable cardiac arrest scenario requiring ongoing advanced cardiac life support was simulated, while airway management, medication administration, cardiac monitoring, and chest compressions continued uninterrupted. Central venous cannulation was successfully completed in all simulations using standard sterile technique. The technical aspects of cannulation were largely unchanged from hospital-based practice, and left femoral venous access was identified as the most practical site. The primary challenges were limited workspace and unfavorable ergonomics related to the fixed stretcher height, which required the operator performing cannulation to work in an awkward position. Despite these constraints, all major advanced cardiac life support interventions were maintained throughout the procedure. These findings suggest that central venous cannulation during ongoing cardiac arrest resuscitation is technically feasible within a standard ambulance environment and support further investigation into advanced vascular access procedures in prehospital critical care.

articles.title: Missed abdominal injuries on initial trauma CT: pitfalls, mimickers and practical pearls.
articles.abstract: Missed and misinterpreted injuries on the initial trauma CT remain a major source of delayed diagnosis and preventable morbidity. This pictorial essay illustrates, with cases from our department, the abdominal injuries most often overlooked: bowel and mesenteric injury, diaphragmatic rupture, hepatic and splenic vascular injury, renal vascular injury, pancreatic injury and bladder rupture. For each, we show the subtle direct and indirect CT signs, the mimickers that lead to over- or under-calling (including unidentified bright objects of the spleen), and the roles of multiphasic CT, multiplanar reformats, dual-energy CT, MRCP and CT cystography. We close with a practical search strategy and a low threshold for repeat imaging when the clinical course is discordant with the first scan.

articles.title: Correction: Datura stramonium seed ingestion leading to unintentional poisoning in a 3-year-old Ethiopian toddler: case report.
Rural iowa adolescents' use, knowledge and attitudes regarding UTVs on public roads.
articles.abstract: Manufacturers specify that utility task vehicles (UTVs) are designed exclusively for off-road operation and are unsuitable for public roadways. Despite this, a growing number of U.S. legislative bodies are enacting laws permitting or expanding UTV access to public roads, creating a significant misalignment between vehicle design intent and actual use environments. Our study objective was to examine rural adolescents' use, knowledge and attitudes regarding UTVs on public roads. Iowa FFA (formerly Future Farmers of America) Leadership Conference attendees were anonymously surveyed from April 15-16, 2024. They were questioned about their UTV use and attitudes regarding UTVs on public roadways, both paved and unpaved. Descriptive, bivariate and logistic regression analyses were performed using Stata 15.1. 1,029 FFA members (13-18 yrs) participated; 50% from farms, 20% from the country/not farms, and 30% from towns. 53% of respondents' families owned UTVs and 69% of respondents had driven/ridden one. Among UTV drivers/riders, 94% had been on unpaved roads (51% at least weekly) and 87% had been on paved roads (41% at least weekly). Overall, 64% and 63% stated it was safe to drive UTVs on unpaved and paved public roads, respectively. 63% stated UTVs were designed for unpaved roads and 54% stated UTVs were designed for paved roads. Over half agreed that manufacturers state UTVs are safe for unpaved (54%) and paved (52%) roads. Generally, males, older teens, UTV owners, UTV riders, those who had ridden on public roads and more frequent riders all had greater proportions holding these misconceptions. The vast majority of respondents (82%) incorrectly believed youth < 18 years old could legally drive UTVs on Iowa's county roads. Most study participants reported UTV operation on public roads and perceived the practice as safe on both paved and unpaved roadway surfaces. They also believed the misconceptions that UTVs are designed for roadways and that manufacturers state UTVs are safe on public roads. The powersports industry should do more to publicize the hazards of off-road vehicles on public roads. Targeted education and evidence-based legislation with enforcement prohibiting on-road operation may be critical in decreasing UTV-related deaths and injuries.

articles.title: Acute fractures and mimics in adult musculoskeletal radiographs.
articles.abstract: Radiographs are the first line imaging modality in evaluation for fractures, which can be challenging in equivocal cases with findings that mimic fractures. Accurate and quick identification of acute fractures is essential for triage, management, and prevention of complications. At the same time, overcalling a benign finding as a fracture can lead to patient anxiety and further testing that adds health care cost and time. As such, familiarity with fracture mimics is a critical skill for clinicians involved in emergency and acute care settings. This pictorial essay reviews common acute fracture patterns and highlights key imaging features that distinguish acute fractures from benign mimics, primarily through numerous representative cases. The article also provides a framework to address equivocal findings with next steps that can be performed for troubleshooting.

articles.title: Real-World Effectiveness of International Border Health Interventions in Mitigating the Spread of SARS-CoV-2 During the First Years of the COVID-19 Pandemic, 2020-2023: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Many vaccine-related and nonpharmaceutical interventions, including travel-related measures, were established to mitigate the spread of SARS-CoV-2. Some countries began to impose measures on travelers from Wuhan, China, the location of the first identified COVID-19 cases, as early as December 31, 2019. The objective of this systematic review was to assess real-world effectiveness of travel-related measures in mitigating the international spread of SARS-CoV-2 during the declared public health emergency from 2020 to 2023. Inclusion criteria encompassed interventional and observational studies describing international travel-related mitigation measures and their effect on cases, hospitalizations, or deaths. Modeling studies were excluded. Electronic searches were performed using Embase (OVID), Global Health (OVID), CINAHL (EBSCOHost), Cochrane Library, Scopus, Medline (OVID), and World Health Organization COVID-19 Global Literature to identify studies published from January 1, 2020, through February 24, 2023. The ROBINS-I tool was used to assess risk of bias. A total of 37 observational studies met inclusion criteria for the review. Of these, 9 (24%) described quarantine-related interventions, 4 (11%) testing-only interventions, 6 (16%) border closures, 5 (14%) vaccination/immunity-based interventions, and 13 (35%) multiple interventions. Risk of bias was judged to be serious or critical for 14 (38%) of the studies. Comparison groups and outcomes were heterogeneous, but most described a positive effect on improving measured decreasing outcomes of interest. Although significant biases may be associated with these observational studies, international travel-related measures may have been effective in temporarily mitigating the spread of SARS-CoV-2 early in the pandemic. However, many measures became less effective as SARS-CoV-2 spread globally. In future pandemics, countries should consider designing evaluation strategies when measures are planned, before implementation.

articles.title: A Case Series and Systematic Review of the Literature of Travelers Who Flew on Commercial Aircraft while Infected With Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers, 2004-2023.
articles.abstract: Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs), specifically those that spread from person to person, have high mortality rates ranging from 17% to 89%, and outbreaks are a cause for international concern. While instances of translocation of VHFs via air travel have been documented, there have been no reported cases of transmission during air travel. We aimed to synthesize available data on travelers who flew while infected with VHFs to assess the risk of transmission during air travel through a systematic review and case series. Eight scholarly databases were searched for studies published from January 2004 to December 2023, describing VHF-infected travelers on commercial flights and resultant contact investigations. We excluded studies that were not original research, did not describe VHFs, or did not have full-text availability. Studies were imported into Covidence, which facilitated abstract screening, full-text review, and data extraction. Additionally, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Port Health Activity Reporting System (PHARS) database (previously the Quarantine Activity Reporting System, or QARS) was searched and reports of travelers who flew while infected with VHFs from 2005-2024 were extracted. Six studies and 4 PHARS reports were identified that described 7 travelers who flew while infected with VHFs. Two cases were symptomatic with wet symptoms (ie, diarrhea or vomiting) during travel, while the remaining 5 cases only had dry symptoms (ie, fever, myalgias), no symptoms, or unknown symptoms. None reported bleeding during travel. In 1 instance, transmission occurred after travel. While translocation of VHFs via commercial air travel has been documented, transmission during air travel has not. The small number of included cases limits generalizability of the findings.

articles.title: Performance of ChatGPT-5 under a minimal binary prompt for detection of distal radius fractures on plain radiographs.
articles.abstract: General-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) are being applied to radiology, but their performance under the simplest realistic clinical query (a single binary fracture-or-not prompt) has not been rigorously quantified. We evaluated ChatGPT-5 on this task using a public distal radius dataset. In this retrospective diagnostic accuracy study, 396 anteroposterior distal radius radiographs from the Stanford MURA dataset were submitted to ChatGPT-5, each in a fresh temporary chat session. The prompt was: "Is there a fracture in this X-ray? Answer with yes or no." The reference standard was an image-level label assigned by consensus between a senior orthopedic resident and a board-certified orthopedic surgeon; MURA study-level labels were used only to select candidate images. Twenty-six radiographs (6.6%) returned a hedged response and were excluded from the primary analysis, leaving 370; all 26 were added back in three sensitivity analyses. Outcomes were sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1, balanced accuracy, and Cohen's kappa, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals and McNemar's test for error asymmetry. Fracture prevalence in the analyzed sample was 45.9% (170/370). Sensitivity was 51.2% (95% CI 43.7-58.6), specificity 70.5% (63.8-76.4), accuracy 61.6% (56.6-66.4), PPV 59.6% (51.5-67.2), NPV 62.9% (56.5-69.0), F1 0.551, Cohen's kappa 0.219 (0.112-0.318). False negatives exceeded false positives (McNemar χ2 = 4.06, p = 0.044). Non-binary responses occurred in 7.6% of fracture-positive and 5.7% of fracture-negative radiographs (p = 0.54); counting all as errors lowered sensitivity to 47.3% (40.2-54.5), and no assumption raised it above 54.9%. Projected to 20% prevalence, PPV was 30.3% and NPV 85.2%. Under a minimal binary prompt and without task-specific fine-tuning, ChatGPT-5 missed approximately half of distal radius fractures and fell well below published performance for dedicated CNN-based fracture detectors. Results are specific to this model version, this prompt, this anatomical region, and this dataset; they constrain claims about autonomous, minimal-prompt use rather than the broader potential of engineered LLM-based radiological workflows.

articles.title: A Study of Staff Experiences of Delivering Prehospital Emergency Services in India in the Context of the EMS Agenda 2050 Objectives.
articles.abstract: Emergency care services are crucial to the delivery of modern healthcare. This study investigated prehospital staff experiences in delivering emergency care in a low- to middle-income country (LMIC) India. The study was guided by the EMS Agenda 2050 principles for people-centred and technology-enabled health systems. The study was performed with emergency medical staff from the city of Gandhinagar, India, which is designated as a future smart city. This research used purposive and snowball sampling with 23 participants (ambulance drivers, emergency medical technicians, paramedics and first-aiders) from government, non-governmental and private organisations. Online semistructured interviews explored current prehospital care practices, challenges and opportunities. NVivo software was used for qualitative analysis, with a reflexive thematic analysis approach used to derive themes and present findings. The thematic analysis identified four primary themes with subthemes: (1) job satisfaction and challenges, (2) attitudes and emotions, (3) technological factors and (4) efficiency and caring. Findings highlight opportunities for technological interventions to enhance citizen awareness and training, support relatives during emergencies, provide bystanders with medically safe guidance and facilitate digitalisation in prehospital care. This research advances understanding of the human and operational realities of prehospital care in a future smart-city context. Healthcare professionals demonstrated expertise and empathy in managing complex emergencies while recognising the importance of their role in caring for critically ill and injured patients. Although digital technologies are increasingly integrated into practice, hands-on skills and experiential judgement remain fundamental to effective care. The findings underscore the need for stakeholder collaboration, enhanced professional training and innovative citizen awareness initiatives to strengthen resilient prehospital care systems.

articles.title: Clinical Characteristics of Spontaneous and Recurrent Pneumomediastinum and Risk Factors of Recurrence.
articles.abstract: Spontaneous pneumomediastinum (SPM) is rare, and most existing knowledge comes from small case series. Although usually benign, SPM often leads to hospital admission and substantial healthcare resource use. This study aimed to characterize SPM and recurrent spontaneous pneumomediastinum (RSPM) in a large cohort and to explore factors associated with recurrence. Patients with SPM hospitalized at Putian First Hospital between September 2011 and September 2023 were included. Clinical data were extracted from electronic medical records. Follow-up was performed to identify RSPM. Patients were divided into nonrecurrence and recurrence groups, and risk factors for recurrence were evaluated using univariate logistic regression. A total of 135 patients with SPM were included. Most patients were male (78.1%), with a median age of 20 years (interquartile range [IQR]: 17-32). A bimodal age distribution was observed, with peaks at 15-19 and 50-54 years. The most common symptom was chest pain (51.9%), and 54.0% of the patients had no identifiable trigger. Among the 9 patients with RSPM (6.7%), median age at recurrence was 25 years (IQR: 16-56) and median interval to recurrence was 6.5 months (range: 1-16.5). Dyspnea was the most common symptom at recurrence (66.7%), and 44.4% of the patients showed greater clinical and radiological severity than at initial presentation. Univariate analysis suggested that a history of bronchitis was associated with RSPM (OR: 11.71, 95% CI: 1.68-81.89); other potential factors included silicosis, pneumonia, and upper respiratory infection as a trigger. SPM predominantly affects young males and generally follows a benign course. Although recurrence is uncommon (6.7%), it may be more severe than the initial episode in nearly half of the cases. A history of bronchitis may be associated with recurrence, but this finding is exploratory. Age-specific preventive strategies and careful exclusion of secondary pneumomediastinum are essential.
